summary.big_en: Every digit has a value that depends on its place. Rounding replaces a number with a nearby simpler one.

topics.title: Place value
topics.subtitle: value | position
topics.def: The place value of a digit is the value it has because of its position in the number.
rules: Understand the value of each digit in a decimal number.
Moving a digit one place to the left makes it ten times bigger.

topics.title: Compose, decompose, regroup
topics.def: Composing builds a number from its parts, decomposing breaks it back down, and regrouping writes the same total a different way.
rules: Write a number in expanded form (compose).
Break a number into its place values (decompose).
Group the values a different way, keeping the same total (regroup).

topics.title: Word form
topics.subtitle: read & write
topics.def: Word form is a number written out in words instead of digits.
rules: Write and read decimal numbers in words.
After the decimal point, say the digits one by one.

topics.title: Multiply & divide by 10, 100, 1000
topics.def: Multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1000 slides every digit along the place value columns.
rules: Multiply or divide a decimal number by 10, 100 or 1000.
Every digit moves 1, 2 or 3 places: left to multiply, right to divide.

topics.title: Rounding
topics.subtitle: rounding off
topics.def: Rounding replaces a number with the nearest simpler number in the place you choose.
rules: Round a number with 2 decimal places to the nearest tenth or whole number.
Look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to.

branches.when: Nearest tenth · hundredths digit is 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
Nearest tenth · hundredths digit is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
branches.then: keep the tenths digit the same

branches.when: Nearest whole number · tenths digit is 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
Nearest whole number · tenths digit is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
branches.then: keep the ones digit the same

glossary.def: One of the symbols 0 to 9 that a number is written with.
glossary.example: The digit 7 in 213.807 stands for 7 thousandths (p.13).

glossary.def: The value a digit has because of its position in the number.
glossary.example: In 6703.46 the 7 has a place value of 7 hundreds (p.13).

glossary.def: The dot that separates the whole-number part from the part smaller than one.
glossary.example: In 13.136 it comes after the 13 (p.13).

glossary.def: The first place after the decimal point.
glossary.example: In 13.136 the 1 after the point is 1 tenth (p.13).

glossary.def: The second place after the decimal point.
glossary.example: In 13.136 the 3 is 3 hundredths (p.13).

glossary.def: The third place after the decimal point.
glossary.example: In 13.136 the 6 is 6 thousandths (p.13).

glossary.def: Putting parts together to make a number.
glossary.example: 3 + 10 + 1 tenth + 3 hundredths + 6 thousandths makes 13.136 (p.13).

glossary.def: Splitting a number into the parts it is made of.
Writing the same number as a different set of parts.
glossary.example: 56.079 is also 56 ones and 79 thousandths (WB p.9).

glossary.def: Replace a number with a nearby number that is easier to use.
glossary.example: 9.63 seconds rounds to 10 seconds (p.16).

glossary.def: The closest of the possible answers.
glossary.example: $14.65 to the nearest dollar is $15 (p.16).

glossary.def: A number written with a decimal point, so it can show parts smaller than one.
glossary.example: A butterfly wingspan of 0.375 inches (p.12).

summary.big_en: A sequence follows a rule. Knowing the rule lets you find any term without writing them all out.

topics.title: Counting on and counting back
topics.def: Counting on and back means adding or subtracting the same amount each time to make a sequence.
rules: Count forward and backward in steps of constant size.
The step can be a fraction or a decimal, not just a whole number.

topics.title: Position to term rule
topics.def: A position-to-term rule turns a term's position number straight into the term itself.
rules: A term-to-term rule tells you the next term; a position-to-term rule tells you any term.
Use the position-to-term rule to jump straight to a far-off term.

topics.title: Square numbers
topics.def: A square number is what you get when you multiply a number by itself.
rules: Work out the square number in any position: the ninth square number is 9 × 9 = 81.
Use the small 2 notation to mean squared.

topics.title: Cube numbers
topics.def: A cube number is what you get when you multiply a number by itself three times.
rules: Know the cube of numbers up to 5.
Cubing means multiplying a number by itself three times.

topics.title: Common multiples and common factors
topics.def: A common multiple is shared by the times tables of two numbers; a common factor divides exactly into both.
rules: A common multiple is in the times table of both numbers.
A common factor divides into both numbers exactly.

glossary.def: One of the numbers in a sequence.
glossary.example: In 2, 4, 6, 8 the third term is 6 (p.22).

glossary.def: Where a term sits in the sequence: first, second, third and so on.
glossary.example: The 25th term is in position 25 (p.22).

glossary.def: A rule that takes you from one term to the next.
glossary.example: First term 4, rule add 7 (p.20).

glossary.def: A rule that gives the term from its position.
glossary.example: Multiply the position by 2, so the 50th term is 100 (p.23).

glossary.def: The result of multiplying a number by itself.
glossary.example: The ninth square number is 9 × 9 = 81 (p.27).

glossary.def: The result of multiplying a number by itself three times.
A number in another number's times table.
glossary.example: 24 is a multiple of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24 (p.30).

glossary.def: A number that divides into another number exactly.
glossary.example: The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18 (p.32).

glossary.def: A multiple that two or more numbers share.
glossary.example: 24 is a common multiple of 3 and 8 (p.30).

glossary.def: A factor that two or more numbers share.
glossary.example: The common factors of 18 and 24 are 1, 2, 3 and 6 (p.32).

summary.big_en: An average is one number that stands for a whole set of data. The range says how spread out the data is.

topics.title: Mode
topics.def: The mode is the value that appears most often in a set of data.
rules: Find the value that comes up most often.
A set with two modes is bimodal; a set where nothing repeats has no mode.

topics.title: Median
topics.def: The median is the middle value once the data is put in order.
rules: Put every value in order from smallest to largest.
With an even number of values, take the two in the middle and find the number halfway between them.

topics.title: Mean
topics.def: The mean is the total of all the values shared equally between them.
rules: Add up every value in the set.
Divide the total by how many values there are.

topics.title: Range
topics.def: The range is the difference between the largest and the smallest value.
rules: Subtract the smallest value from the largest.
A big range means the data is spread out; a small range means it is close together.

topics.title: Using averages to describe data
topics.def: An average represents what is typical for a set of data, so it helps you compare two sets and make decisions.
rules: Use the average and the range together to describe a set of data.
One very large or very small value can pull the mean away from what is typical.

lines: Watch out: the one $263 bucket pulls the mean up

glossary.def: One number that represents a whole set of data.
glossary.example: A book scored an average of 6 out of 10 by its reviewers (p.39).

glossary.def: The value that appears most often.
glossary.example: In 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7 the modes are 4 and 5 (p.40).

glossary.def: Having two modes.
The middle value when the data is put in order.
glossary.example: In 4, 4, 5, 7, 10 the median is 5 (p.40).

glossary.def: The total of the values divided by how many there are.
The difference between the largest and smallest value.

summary.big_en: Integers go below zero as well as above. A letter can stand for a number you do not know yet.

topics.title: Positive and negative integers
topics.def: An integer is a whole number, and it can be positive, negative or zero.
rules: Numbers below zero are negative and are written with a minus sign.
On a number line, moving right adds and moving left subtracts.

topics.title: Estimate, add and subtract large integers
topics.def: Estimating means rounding the numbers first so you can check whether an answer is sensible.
rules: Round each number, then add or subtract the rounded numbers.
Compare the estimate with the exact answer to spot mistakes.

lines: Check: 8,015 is close to 8,000, so it is sensible

topics.title: Difference between two integers
topics.def: The difference between two integers is how far apart they are on the number line.
rules: Count the steps from one number to the other.
When one number is negative and the other positive, count up to zero and then on.

example.title: Temperatures
lines: From −6 to 4: 6 steps to zero, then 4 more

topics.title: Using letters to represent numbers
topics.def: A letter can stand for a number, so you can write a rule without knowing the number yet.
rules: Replace the letter with its value to work the expression out.
Addition can be written either way round, but subtraction cannot.

topics.title: Constants and variables
topics.def: A constant always has the same value, while a variable can take different values.
rules: An unknown is not always one fixed number: it can be a variable.
List the possible pairs of values when two letters must add to a fixed total.

example.title: Rectangle with perimeter 20 cm
lines: Rule: s + t is half of 20, so s + t = 10

glossary.def: A whole number, which can be positive, negative or zero.
glossary.example: −30 and 550 are both integers (p.49).

glossary.def: A number greater than zero.
glossary.example: A depth of 550 m below the surface (p.49).

glossary.def: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign.
glossary.example: A temperature of −30 °C (p.50).

glossary.def: How far apart two numbers are.
glossary.example: The difference in temperature between two cities (p.51).

glossary.def: A value that always stays the same.
glossary.example: The perimeter stays 20 cm (p.55).

glossary.def: A letter standing for a value that can change.
glossary.example: d is the dice score, so it changes each throw (p.55).

glossary.def: A rough answer worked out by rounding the numbers first.
A rule written with numbers and letters, such as d + 4.
glossary.example: When the dice score d is 5, d + 4 is 9 (p.55).

summary.big_en: Every 2D shape can be described by its properties: a quadrilateral by its sides, angles and diagonals, and a circle by its centre and radius. Rotational symmetry counts how many times a shape looks the same in one full turn.

topics.title: QUADRILATERALS
topics.subtitle: sides | angles | diagonals
topics.def: A quadrilateral is a 2D shape with four straight sides.
rules: Describe a quadrilateral by its sides, its angles, its diagonals and its lines of symmetry.
Marks on a diagram show the properties: matching dashes for equal sides, matching arrows for parallel sides and a small square for a 90 degree angle.
Quadrilateral tiles tessellate, which means they fit together exactly leaving no spaces.

example.title: Properties of a rectangle
lines: Sides: four, so it is a quadrilateral
Angles: the sides meet at 90 degrees
Lines of symmetry: 2, one horizontal and one vertical

topics.title: THE SEVEN SPECIAL QUADRILATERALS
topics.def: The seven special quadrilaterals are the square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, isosceles trapezium, rhombus and kite.
rules: Classify a quadrilateral by ticking which properties it has: equal sides, parallel sides, equal angles and how the diagonals behave.
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides; an isosceles trapezium also has one pair of equal sides.
The diagonals of a kite meet at 90 degrees, and a rhombus has two pairs of equal angles.

topics.title: PARTS OF A CIRCLE
topics.subtitle: centre | radius | diameter
topics.def: A circle is the set of points that are all the same distance from a centre point.
rules: The radius joins the centre to the circumference; the diameter joins two points on the circumference and passes through the centre.
The circumference is the perimeter of the circle, the distance all the way round it.
The diameter is twice the radius, so a radius of 3 cm gives a diameter of 60 mm.

example.title: Cards that give the same size circle
lines: Radius 2 cm = radius 20 mm = diameter 4 cm
Radius 4 cm = radius 40 mm = diameter 8 cm
Radius 10 cm = diameter 20 cm = diameter 200 mm

topics.title: DRAWING CIRCLES ACCURATELY
topics.def: You draw a circle by opening a pair of compasses to the radius and turning them round a centre dot.
rules: Open the compasses against a ruler to the radius, mark the centre with a dot, put the point on it and turn the compasses carefully.
Remember that 1 cm = 10 mm, so a radius of 60 mm means opening the compasses to 6 cm.
A diameter must be drawn through the centre; a line joining two points on the circumference that misses the centre is not a diameter.

example.title: Two circles that touch
lines: Distance between the two centres: 8.5 cm

topics.title: ROTATIONAL SYMMETRY
topics.subtitle: order
topics.def: A shape has rotational symmetry if it can be rotated about a point to another position and still look the same.
rules: The order of rotational symmetry is the number of times the shape looks the same in one full turn.
Every shape looks the same again after a full turn, so the smallest order is 1; order 1 means the shape has no rotational symmetry.
Tracing paper helps: trace the shape, then turn the tracing about the centre and count the positions where it fits.

branches.when: It only fits back on itself after a full turn
It also fits after a half turn
It fits three times in one full turn
It fits four times in one full turn

glossary.def: Cut exactly in half.
glossary.example: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other (p.64).

glossary.def: A line that joins opposite corners of a quadrilateral.
glossary.example: The two diagonals of a square meet at 90 degrees (p.65).

glossary.def: Lines that never meet and always stay the same distance apart.
glossary.example: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides (p.65).

glossary.def: Give a reason for your answer.
glossary.example: Side a is parallel to g because both are parallel to e (p.68).

glossary.def: The plural of trapezium.
glossary.example: Trapezia can be sorted into those that are isosceles and those that are not (p.66).

glossary.def: The middle point of a circle.
glossary.example: Put the point of the compasses on the centre before you turn them (p.71).

glossary.def: The perimeter of a circle, the distance all the way round it.
glossary.example: A diameter joins two points on the circumference (p.70).

glossary.def: A line joining the centre of a circle to the circumference.
glossary.example: Arun draws a circle with a radius of 3 cm (p.73).

glossary.def: A line joining two points on the circumference that passes through the centre.
glossary.example: A circle with a diameter of 60 mm has a radius of 3 cm (p.73).

glossary.def: An instrument used to draw circles.
glossary.example: Open your compasses to 4 cm to draw a circle of radius 4 cm (p.71).

glossary.def: When a shape can be turned about a point to a new position and still look the same.
glossary.example: A rectangle has rotational symmetry of order 2 (p.76).

glossary.def: The number of times a shape looks the same in one full turn.
glossary.example: A button made of four identical parts has order 4 (p.76).

summary.big_en: A fraction is another way of writing a division, and it can also act as an operator that finds part of an amount. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways of writing the same value, so any of them can be compared once they are in the same form.

topics.title: PROPER, IMPROPER AND MIXED
topics.subtitle: numerator | denominator
topics.def: A proper fraction is smaller than one whole, an improper fraction is one whole or more, and a mixed number is a whole number written next to a proper fraction.
rules: The numerator is the top number and the denominator is the bottom number.
A fraction is another way of writing a division, so 5 divided by 6 is written 5/6.
An improper fraction can be rewritten as a mixed number, because the whole ones can be taken out of it.

example.title: The improper fraction 7/4
lines: Numerator is bigger, so it is greater than one whole

topics.title: FRACTIONS AS OPERATORS
topics.def: Using a fraction as an operator means using it to find that fraction of an amount.
rules: Divide the amount by the denominator, then multiply the result by the numerator.
An improper fraction is used in exactly the same way, but the answer is bigger than the amount you started with.

example.title: Which is bigger, 3/4 of 20 or 4/3 of 12?
lines: So 4/3 of 12 is the bigger one

topics.title: PERCENTAGES
topics.subtitle: per cent = parts per hundred
topics.def: A percentage is an amount written as a number of parts out of every hundred, using the % sign.
rules: 10% is the same as 1/10, so divide by 10 to find 10%, then multiply that answer to build the percentage you need.
50% is a half, so you divide by 2 and not by 5.
Always write the units in the answer, such as cm, kg or dollars.

topics.title: SIMPLEST FORM
topics.def: A fraction is in its simplest form when the numerator and the denominator cannot both be divided by the same number again.
rules: Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number, and repeat until no common number is left.
Simplifying does not change the value of the fraction, only the numbers used to write it.

example.title: Simplify 4/20
lines: 1 and 5 have no common number left

topics.title: EQUIVALENCE AND COMPARISON
topics.def: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways of writing the same value, so one can be changed into another in order to compare them.
rules: A fraction with a denominator of 100 becomes a percentage straight away, so 3/100 is 3%.
A fraction with a denominator of 10 becomes tenths as a decimal, so 7/10 is 0.7.
To put a mixed list in order, change every number into the same form first, then compare them.

glossary.def: The top number of a fraction.
glossary.example: In 7/4 the numerator is 7 (p.85).

glossary.def: The bottom number of a fraction, showing how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
glossary.example: In 7/4 the denominator is 4 (p.85).

glossary.def: A fraction smaller than one whole, where the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
glossary.example: 3/4 of 20 uses the proper fraction 3/4 (p.85).

glossary.def: A fraction equal to or greater than one whole, where the numerator is at least as big as the denominator.
glossary.example: 7/4 is an improper fraction (p.85).

glossary.def: A whole number and a proper fraction written together.
glossary.example: 7/4 is the same as the mixed number 1 3/4 (p.85).

glossary.def: A fraction used to find that fraction of an amount.
glossary.example: Finding 6/5 of a number uses the fraction as an operator (p.86).

glossary.def: The number of parts out of every hundred.
glossary.example: 10% off a jumper costing $20 takes $2 off the price (p.88).

glossary.def: An amount written as a number of parts per hundred, using the % sign.
glossary.example: A shop offers 25% off in its sale (p.88).

glossary.def: Reduce the numerator and the denominator of a fraction to smaller numbers.
glossary.example: 12/20 simplifies to 3/5 (p.93).

glossary.def: A fraction whose numerator and denominator cannot be reduced any further.
glossary.example: 1/5 is the simplest form of 4/20 (p.92).

glossary.def: A fraction that has exactly the same value as another fraction.
glossary.example: 6/10 and 60/100 are equivalent fractions, both equal to 0.6 (p.94).

summary.big_en: Area is the size of the surface a shape covers: a rectangle's area is its length times its width, and a triangle cut from a rectangle covers half of it. A length of time can be written as a decimal number of hours or in mixed units, and 0.1 of an hour is 6 minutes.

topics.title: AREA OF A RECTANGLE
topics.subtitle: Length × width
topics.def: Area is the size of the surface a shape covers, and it is measured in square units such as cm² and m².
rules: Multiply the width by the length to find the area of a rectangle.
Always write area in square units. The units come from the lengths you measured, so metres give m² and centimetres give cm².

example.title: A rectangle 8 m long and 4 m wide

topics.title: COUNTING SQUARES
topics.subtitle: Estimating an area
topics.def: Counting the squares of a grid is a way of estimating the area of a shape whose sides do not follow the grid lines, such as a triangle.
rules: Count every square the shape covers completely.
Count a square that is about half covered as half a square, and put the other part squares together to make whole ones.

example.title: A triangle inside a rectangle 8 cm by 4 cm
lines: The triangle is as wide and as tall as the rectangle
Every triangle drawn this way covers about half the rectangle

topics.title: AREA OF A TRIANGLE
topics.subtitle: Half of a rectangle
topics.def: A triangle made by cutting a rectangle in half along a diagonal has exactly half the area of that rectangle.
rules: Work out the area of the whole rectangle first, then divide it by 2.
This works backwards too: double the area of the triangle to get the area of the rectangle it came from.

topics.title: HOURS AS DECIMALS
topics.def: The same length of time can be written as a decimal number of hours or in mixed units of hours and minutes, and the two forms mean exactly the same thing.
rules: Keep the whole number part as whole hours.
Multiply the part after the point by 60 to change it into minutes. One tenth of an hour is 6 minutes, so 0.7 of an hour is 7 × 6 = 42 minutes.

topics.title: SHARING AND CONVERTING TIMES
topics.def: When a length of time is shared out or divided, the answer often comes out as a decimal that has to be converted into mixed units before it makes sense.
rules: Divide the time first, then convert the part after the point into minutes.
12.5 hours is not 12 hours and 5 minutes. The figures after the point are parts of an hour, so 0.5 of an hour is 30 minutes.

branches.when: The part after the point is 0.25 of an hour
branches.eg: 5 hours shared by 4 = 1.25 hours → 1 hour and 15 minutes

branches.when: The part after the point is 0.4 of an hour
branches.eg: 12 hours shared by 5 = 2.4 hours → 2 hours and 24 minutes

branches.when: The time is a decimal number of minutes
branches.then: Multiply the part after the point by 60 to get seconds

glossary.def: The size of the surface a shape covers, measured in square units such as cm² and m².
glossary.example: A rectangle 8 m by 4 m has an area of 32 m² (p.104).

glossary.def: A unit of area the size of a square measuring 1 cm by 1 cm, written cm².
glossary.example: The triangles are drawn on a centimetre square grid, so each square is 1 cm² (p.102).

glossary.def: A length of time from a starting point to an ending point.
glossary.example: 3.7 hours is a time interval written as a decimal (p.107).

glossary.def: A time written with more than one unit together, such as hours and minutes.
glossary.example: 3.7 hours in mixed units is 3 hours and 42 minutes (p.107).

glossary.def: A triangle with one angle of 90°.
glossary.example: Cutting a rectangle along its diagonal makes two right-angled triangles (p.103).

summary.big_en: Decimals are added and subtracted by keeping digits of the same value in the same column, using trailing zeros so both numbers have the same number of decimal places. Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they have been rewritten with a common denominator.

topics.title: DECOMPOSING DECIMALS
topics.subtitle: Breaking a number into its parts
topics.def: Decomposing a decimal means breaking it into the value of each of its digits, and composing means putting those values back together again.
rules: Each digit after the point is worth ten times less than the one before it: 0.8, then 0.04, then 0.004.
You can also regroup a number to write it a different way, for example 10 as 9 + 0.9 + 0.1, so that there is enough to subtract from.

topics.title: ADDING AND SUBTRACTING DECIMALS
topics.subtitle: Line up the point
topics.def: Decimals are added and subtracted in the same way as whole numbers, as long as digits with the same value are kept in the same column.
rules: Line up the decimal points, and write trailing zeros so that both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Estimate the answer first, then check your result against the estimate to see whether it is sensible.

topics.title: COMMON DENOMINATORS
topics.def: A common denominator is a number that both denominators divide into, so that two fractions can be rewritten with parts of the same size.
rules: List the multiples of each denominator and choose a number that appears in both lists.
Change each fraction into an equivalent fraction with that denominator; the fraction is worth the same as before.

topics.title: ADDING AND SUBTRACTING FRACTIONS
topics.def: Two fractions can only be added or subtracted when they have the same denominator; then you add or subtract the numerators and keep that denominator.
rules: Only the numerators are added or subtracted. The denominator stays the same.
Simplify the answer if you can, and change an improper fraction into a mixed number.
To find a missing part of a whole, add the parts you know, then subtract that total from the whole.

example.title: Leroy colours 1/4 and 1/6 of a circle

glossary.def: The position of a digit to the right of the decimal point.
glossary.example: 37.844 has three decimal places (p.115).

glossary.def: A zero written at the end of a decimal so that two numbers have the same number of decimal places.
glossary.example: 10 is written as 10.00 before subtracting 7.58 (p.115).

glossary.def: A number that both denominators divide into, so two fractions can be written with parts of the same size.
glossary.example: 20 is a common denominator for 9/5 and 3/4 (p.118).

glossary.def: Fractions that are worth the same amount, even though they are written differently.
glossary.example: 3/4 and 15/20 are equivalent fractions (p.118).

glossary.def: Fractions that already share the same denominator, so they can be added straight away.
glossary.example: 3/8 and 2/8 are like fractions (p.119).

summary.big_en: Probability is a number that says how likely an event is to happen, and it can be written as a fraction or as a percentage. Once you know the likelihood of each outcome you can predict what will most likely happen, and two events that cannot happen at the same time are mutually exclusive.

topics.title: DESCRIBING CHANCE
topics.subtitle: Fractions and percentages
topics.def: Probability is a number that shows how likely an event is to happen, and it can be written as a fraction or as a percentage instead of in words.
rules: Write the number of outcomes you want above the total number of outcomes there are.
A percentage says how many parts out of every hundred, so 5 out of 10 is 50%. Something certain is 100% and something impossible cannot happen at all.

rows: Taking a card that is not a 3

topics.title: MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE EVENTS
topics.def: Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot happen at the same time.
rules: Look for one single outcome that fits both events. If you can find one, the events are not mutually exclusive.
Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so there is no chance at all of both happening together.

branches.when: Spin a 5 and spin a number greater than 2
Spin a number greater than 2 and spin a number less than 4
branches.eg: a 3 is greater than 2 and less than 4

branches.when: Spin a 5 and spin a number less than 4
branches.eg: no number is both 5 and less than 4

topics.title: PREDICTING OUTCOMES
topics.def: If you know how likely each outcome is, you can predict roughly how many times each one will happen in a given number of trials.
rules: Write each outcome as a fraction of the trials, then keep that same fraction when the number of trials changes.
A prediction only says what is most likely to happen. The real results can still be different.

topics.title: CHANCE EXPERIMENTS
topics.def: A probability experiment is a set of trials carried out to find out how often each outcome really happens.
rules: Record the outcome of every trial in a tally chart, then count the totals.
The experimental probability is the number of times an outcome happened out of the total number of trials.
A large number of trials shows the likelihood of an event much better than a small number of trials.

example.title: Keran flips a coin and tallies the results
lines: Experimental probability of tails: 16 out of 40

glossary.def: A number that shows the chance of an event happening.
glossary.example: The probability of taking a 2 from ten cards is 1/10, or 10% (p.125).

glossary.def: Outcomes that have the same probability as each other.
glossary.example: A coin is equally likely to land heads up or tails up (p.122).

glossary.def: One or more outcomes grouped together and described in one sentence.
glossary.example: 'The spinner lands on a number less than 6' is an event (p.131).

glossary.def: Events that cannot happen at the same time.
glossary.example: Spinning a 5 and spinning a number less than 4 are mutually exclusive (p.126).

glossary.def: How likely an event is to happen, from impossible up to certain.
glossary.example: Asubi uses likelihood to predict that a spinner lands on red 4 times in 8 spins (p.129).

glossary.def: The result of one trial in a probability experiment.
glossary.example: Heads up and tails up are the two outcomes of flipping a coin (p.125).

glossary.def: A situation where a number of trials are carried out to explore probability.
glossary.example: Keran flipped a coin 40 times and recorded the results in a tally chart (p.125).

summary.big_en: Estimate first, calculate with a written method, then check the answer against the estimate. Tests of divisibility tell you quickly whether a division will come out exactly.

topics.title: ESTIMATE AND CHECK
topics.subtitle: before and after
topics.def: An estimate is a quick rough answer worked out with easier numbers, used to check that the real answer is a sensible size.
rules: Round the numbers to ones that are easy to multiply or divide, then calculate.
For a division, round both the dividend and the divisor.
Compare the real answer with the estimate; if they are far apart, check the working.

topics.title: MULTIPLICATION
topics.subtitle: finding a product
topics.def: Multiplying combines equal groups, and the answer you get is called the product.
rules: Multiply the ones first, then the tens, hundreds and thousands, carrying into the next column.
To multiply by a multiple of 10, multiply by the digit and then by 10.
To multiply by a 2-digit number, split it into tens and ones and add the two partial answers.

topics.title: DIVISION
topics.subtitle: dividend | divisor | quotient
topics.def: Dividing shares the dividend into equal groups the size of the divisor, and the answer is the quotient.
rules: Start with an estimate by rounding the dividend and the divisor.
Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, tens first and then ones, until nothing is left.
You can also divide in two steps using factors of the divisor.

topics.title: REMAINDERS
topics.def: A remainder is the amount left over when one number does not divide into another exactly.
rules: The leftover can be written after an r, or as a fraction with the divisor underneath.
Check a division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder.

topics.title: TESTS OF DIVISIBILITY
topics.subtitle: 3, 6 and 9
topics.def: A test of divisibility is a quick rule that tells you whether a number divides exactly, without leaving a remainder.
rules: Add up the digits of the number; the digit sum is what the tests for 3 and 9 look at.
A number divisible by 6 is always divisible by 3 as well, so it sits in the overlap on a Venn diagram.

branches.when: the digits add up to a multiple of 3
the digits add up to a multiple of 9
the number is even and divisible by 3

glossary.def: The answer you get when numbers are multiplied together.
glossary.example: The product of 1347 and 8 is 10 776 (p.135).

glossary.def: The number that is being divided.
glossary.example: In 552 ÷ 24 the dividend is 552 (p.139).

glossary.def: The number you are dividing by.
glossary.example: In 552 ÷ 24 the divisor is 24 (p.139).

glossary.def: The answer to a division.
glossary.example: 552 ÷ 24 = 23, so the quotient is 23 (p.139).

glossary.def: The amount left over when a number does not divide exactly.
A number is divisible by another when it divides exactly, with nothing left over.
glossary.example: 43 719 is divisible by 3 (p.143).

glossary.def: A quick rule for deciding whether a number divides exactly, without doing the division.
glossary.example: A number is divisible by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3 (p.142).

glossary.def: Overlapping circles used to sort numbers into groups, with numbers in both groups in the overlap.
glossary.example: 24 goes in the overlap of 'divisible by 3' and 'divisible by 6' (p.143).

glossary.def: The operation that undoes another one.
glossary.example: Check 23 × 4 = 92 by working out 92 ÷ 4 = 23 (p.145).

summary.big_en: A 3D shape can be built from simpler shapes and opened out into a net, and the total area of its faces is its surface area. Capacity is how much a container can hold; volume is how much is really in it.

topics.title: COMPOUND 3D SHAPES
topics.def: A compound shape is a shape made by joining two or more simpler shapes together.
rules: Describe a compound 3D shape by naming the simple shapes it splits into.
There is often more than one correct way to split the same shape.

example.title: A small block sitting on a longer block
lines: One description: a cube and a cuboid
Both are correct: they split the same shape in different places

topics.title: NETS
topics.subtitle: the shape opened out flat
topics.def: A net is a flat pattern of joined faces that folds up to make a 3D shape.
rules: Count the faces first, then draw one face of the right shape and size for each of them.
A shape can have several different nets that all fold up correctly.
A prism has two identical end faces with rectangles joining them.

topics.title: SURFACE AREA
topics.def: The surface area of a 3D shape is the total area of all its faces.
rules: Work out the area of every face, then add all the areas together.
Sketching the net helps because it lays each face out flat.
A cube has six identical square faces, so its surface area is six times the area of one face.

example.title: Finding the surface area of a cuboid
lines: Step 1: sketch the net so every face is flat
Step 2: work out the area of each of the six faces
Step 3: add all six areas together
Shortcut for a cube: 6 × the area of one square face

topics.title: CAPACITY AND VOLUME
topics.subtitle: what it holds | what is in it
topics.def: Capacity is the greatest amount a container can hold, and volume is the amount of space the liquid or object inside actually takes up.
rules: Read the capacity from the top mark of the scale and the volume from the level of the liquid.
A container is full to capacity when the volume equals the capacity.
To find how much more will fit, subtract the volume from the capacity.

example.title: A jug marked up to 600 ml with water at the 500 ml mark

topics.title: READING SCALES
topics.subtitle: litres and millilitres
topics.def: The scale on a jug is a number line up its side, and you read a volume from the mark the liquid reaches.
rules: Work out what one small step on the scale is worth before you read a value.
1 litre = 1000 ml, so 2500 ml is 2 litres 500 ml or 2.5 litres.
To estimate a volume, decide what fraction of the container is full, then work out that fraction of its capacity.

glossary.def: A shape made up of two or more simpler shapes joined together.
glossary.example: A cube joined to a cuboid makes a compound shape (p.149).

glossary.def: A flat pattern of joined faces that folds up to make a 3D shape.
glossary.example: The net of a cuboid has four rectangles and two squares (p.150).

glossary.def: A 3D shape with two identical parallel faces, with rectangles for all the other faces.
glossary.example: A triangular prism has 2 triangular faces and 3 rectangular faces (p.151).

glossary.def: The total area of all the faces of a 3D shape.
glossary.example: The surface area of a cuboid is the area of its six faces added together (p.151).

glossary.def: The greatest amount that a container can hold.
glossary.example: A jug marked up to 600 ml has a capacity of 600 ml (p.154).

glossary.def: The amount of space taken up by an object, liquid or gas.
glossary.example: Water standing at the 500 ml mark has a volume of 500 ml (p.154).

glossary.def: A unit used to measure capacity and volume; one litre is 1000 millilitres.
glossary.example: 2500 ml is the same as 2.5 litres (p.155).

summary.big_en: A ratio compares one part with another part, and it can be scaled up, scaled down or written in its simplest form. Two quantities are in direct proportion when their ratio stays the same.

topics.title: RATIO
topics.subtitle: part to part
topics.def: A ratio is a comparison between two or more quantities that says how many of one thing there are for every so many of another.
rules: Write a ratio with a colon, keeping the quantities in the order they are named.
A ratio compares one part with another part, not with the whole.

example.title: A bowl holding 6 apples and 3 oranges
lines: In words: 2 apples for every 1 orange

topics.title: EQUIVALENT RATIOS
topics.def: Equivalent ratios are ratios that describe the same relationship, made by multiplying or dividing every part by the same number.
rules: Whatever you do to one part of the ratio, do to the other part as well.
To find a missing number, work out what the known part was multiplied by, then do the same to the other part.

example.title: Apples to bananas is 3 : 5 and 45 people chose bananas

topics.title: SIMPLEST FORM
topics.def: A ratio is in its simplest form when its parts cannot be divided any further by the same whole number.
rules: Divide both parts by the largest number that goes into both of them.
It works the same way as writing a fraction in its simplest form.

topics.title: PROPORTION
topics.subtitle: part of the whole
topics.def: A proportion is a part compared with the whole, so it tells you how many out of the total there are.
rules: Ratio compares part to part; proportion compares part to whole.
A proportion can be written as 'x in every y', as a fraction or as a percentage.

example.title: Green paint from 2 cans of blue and 3 cans of yellow
lines: Proportion that is blue: 2 in every 5
As a fraction: 2/5 is blue and 3/5 is yellow
As a percentage: 60% of the paint is yellow

topics.title: DIRECT PROPORTION
topics.subtitle: the ratio stays the same
topics.def: Two quantities are in direct proportion when their ratio stays the same, so as one increases the other increases in the same way.
rules: Work out what the known quantity was multiplied or divided by, then do the same to the other one.
A scale of 1 : 24 means every length on the real object is 24 times the length on the model.
When a shape is enlarged, all its lengths change in the same ratio and its angles stay the same size.

glossary.def: A comparison between two or more quantities that compares part with part.
glossary.example: A bowl of 6 apples and 3 oranges gives the ratio 6 : 3 (p.166).

glossary.def: A ratio that means the same as another, made by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number.
glossary.example: 3 : 5 = 27 : 45, because both parts are multiplied by 9 (p.166).

glossary.def: A part compared with the whole, telling you how many out of the total.
glossary.example: In green paint made from 2 cans of blue and 3 of yellow, 2 in every 5 cans are blue (p.164).

glossary.def: The relationship between two quantities whose ratio stays the same, so when one increases the other increases too.
glossary.example: 1 hour of work earns $20, 2 hours earn $40 and 4 hours earn $80 (p.165).

glossary.def: To make a shape bigger or smaller so that every length changes in the same ratio.
glossary.example: A 5 cm by 2 cm rectangle enlarged in the ratio 1 : 2 becomes 10 cm by 4 cm (p.172).

glossary.def: A ratio that compares the size of a model with the size of the real object.
glossary.example: A scale of 1 : 24 means the real car is 24 times as long as the model (p.172).

glossary.def: A ratio written with the smallest whole numbers possible.
glossary.example: 3 : 12 in its lowest terms is 1 : 4 (p.167).

summary.big_en: Angles are measured in degrees using a protractor. The three angles inside every triangle add up to 180 degrees, so you can work out an angle that is not given.

topics.title: THE PROTRACTOR
topics.subtitle: The tool for angles
topics.def: A protractor is a flat, see-through instrument marked from 0° to 360° around its edge, used for measuring and drawing angles.
rules: A ruler is for measuring and drawing straight lines; a protractor is for measuring and drawing angles.
It is usually made of clear plastic so you can see the angle through it.

topics.title: MEASURING AN ANGLE
topics.def: Measuring an angle means reading off, in degrees, how far one arm has opened away from the other.
rules: Put the centre of the protractor exactly on the point where the two arms meet.
Line one arm up exactly with 0°, then read the number where the other arm crosses the scale.

example.title: Measuring angle x
lines: Centre of protractor: on the point of the angle
Horizontal arm: lined up exactly with 0°
Angle opens: clockwise, so use the outside numbers

topics.title: DRAWING AN ANGLE
topics.def: Drawing an angle means making an angle of a size you have been given, using a ruler for the arms and a protractor for the size.
rules: Start with a horizontal line, then place the centre of the protractor on one end of it with the other end at 0°.
Mark the size you want, join the mark to the end of the line, then add an arc and write the size on the diagram.

example.title: Drawing 120°
lines: Step 1: draw a horizontal line with a ruler
Step 2: centre of protractor on the right end, left end at 0°
Step 3: count 120° clockwise and mark that point
Step 4: join the mark to the end of the line
Step 5: draw an arc and write 120° on it

topics.title: ANGLES IN A TRIANGLE
topics.subtitle: They always make 180°
topics.def: The three angles inside any triangle always add up to 180°, whatever the size or shape of the triangle.
rules: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put the points together: they make a straight line.
To find a missing angle, add the angles you know and subtract that total from 180°.

topics.title: SPECIAL TRIANGLES
topics.def: Equilateral, isosceles and scalene triangles have different numbers of equal angles, and knowing which is which helps you find a missing angle.
rules: An equilateral triangle has three equal angles, so each one is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
An isosceles triangle has two equal angles; the dashes on two sides show which sides, and so which angles, are equal.
A scalene triangle has three angles that are all different sizes.

topics.title: LINES, RIGHT ANGLES AND FULL TURNS
topics.def: Angles that meet at a point on a straight line add up to 180°, and angles all the way round a point add up to 360°.
rules: A right angle is 90° and is marked with a small square symbol.
Use the line rule and the triangle rule together when a triangle sits on a straight line.

branches.when: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line
branches.then: They add up to 180°, so subtract the one you know

branches.when: A triangle sits on a straight line
branches.then: Find the angle inside the triangle first, then use 180° for the triangle

branches.when: Angles go all the way round a point
branches.then: They make a full turn of 360°

glossary.def: An instrument used for measuring and drawing angles.
glossary.example: A protractor is marked from 0° to 360° around its edge (p.178).

glossary.def: Turning in the same direction as the hands of a clock.
glossary.example: An angle that opens clockwise from 0° is read on the outside numbers (p.178).

glossary.def: Turning in the opposite direction to the hands of a clock.
glossary.example: An angle that opens anticlockwise from 0° is read on the inside numbers (p.178).

glossary.def: The small curved line drawn between two arms to show which angle is meant.
glossary.example: After drawing 120° you add an arc and write the size on it (p.179).

glossary.def: A triangle whose three sides are all different lengths and whose three angles are all different sizes.
glossary.example: A triangle with angles 35°, 45° and 100° is scalene (p.186).

glossary.def: A triangle with two sides equal in length and two angles equal in size.
glossary.example: An isosceles triangle with angles of 50° and 50° has a third angle of 80° (p.185).

glossary.def: A triangle with all three sides equal in length and all three angles equal in size.
glossary.example: Each angle in an equilateral triangle is 60° (p.186).

glossary.def: An angle of exactly 90°, marked on a diagram with a small square symbol.
glossary.example: A right-angled triangle with a 28° angle has a third angle of 62° (p.185).

summary.big_en: Multiplying or dividing a fraction by a whole number changes only one part of the fraction. With decimals you estimate first, then use the same column methods as for whole numbers.

topics.title: MULTIPLYING A FRACTION
topics.subtitle: By a whole number
topics.def: Multiplying a proper fraction by a whole number is the same as adding that fraction to itself that many times.
rules: Multiply the numerator by the whole number and leave the denominator as it is.
If the answer is an improper fraction, write it as a mixed number or in a simpler form.

topics.title: DIVIDING A FRACTION
topics.subtitle: By a whole number
topics.def: Dividing a proper fraction by a whole number cuts each of its equal parts into that many smaller equal parts.
rules: Multiply the denominator by the whole number and leave the numerator as it is.
Simplify the answer if the top and bottom numbers can both be made smaller.

lines: Start with 2/3 of a shape shaded
Cut each third into 4 equal parts: 12 parts in the whole
The shaded piece is now 2 parts out of 12: 2/12

topics.title: TIDYING UP A FRACTION ANSWER
topics.def: An answer that comes out as an improper fraction can be rewritten as a mixed number, and any fraction can be written in its simplest form.
rules: An improper fraction has a numerator at least as big as its denominator, so it is worth one whole or more.
A fraction is in its simplest form when the numerator and denominator cannot be made any smaller.

topics.title: MULTIPLYING DECIMALS
topics.subtitle: Estimate, then multiply in parts
topics.def: To multiply a number with decimal places by a whole number you estimate first, then multiply in parts and add the parts together.
rules: Estimate by rounding both numbers, so you know roughly what the answer should be.
Multiply by the ones and by the tens separately, then add the two answers together.
Check that the answer is close to your estimate.

topics.title: DIVIDING DECIMALS
topics.subtitle: Estimate, then take away multiples
topics.def: To divide a number with decimal places by a whole number you estimate first, then take away multiples of the divisor until nothing is left.
rules: Round to numbers that divide easily, and notice whether the real answer will be bigger or smaller than the estimate.
Work down from the ones to the tenths, writing each figure on the answer line.
Check by multiplying the quotient back by the divisor.

lines: Estimate: 50 ÷ 25 = 2, so the answer is a little more than 2

glossary.def: Adding the same number again and again, which is what multiplying by a whole number means.
A fraction with 1 on top, such as 1/4.
glossary.example: Dividing by a whole number splits a fraction into unit fractions (p.195).

glossary.def: One part of a multiplication that is worked out on its own before the parts are added.
glossary.example: For 4 × 3.2, work out 4 × 3 and 4 × 0.2, then add (p.197).

glossary.def: Dividing by writing the calculation out in one line with the remainders carried across.
Divide the top and the bottom of a fraction by the same number to make it simpler.
glossary.example: 6/8 cancels to 3/4 (p.194).

summary.big_en: Data can be shown as bars, dots, slices or points, and the picture you choose depends on the question you are asking. A good graph lets you see a pattern and estimate values you never measured.

topics.title: BAR CHARTS AND DOT PLOTS
topics.def: A bar chart shows frequency with the height of a bar; a dot plot shows it with a column of dots, one dot for each item.
rules: The height of a bar, or the number of dots stacked above a value, is the frequency of that value.
Add every frequency together to find the size of the whole set: 10 + 28 + 29 + 5 = 72 pods.
A bar can stand for one single value or for a group of values such as 1-5 or 6-10.

topics.title: WAFFLE DIAGRAMS
topics.def: A waffle diagram is a rectangle of 100 squares, coloured in so that each category takes the share of the squares that belongs to it.
rules: One square is one per cent of the whole, so counting the coloured squares gives the percentage straight away.
Divide 100 by the number of items counted to find how many squares stand for one item.
Always draw a key saying which colour belongs to which category.

topics.title: PIE CHARTS
topics.def: A pie chart is a circle cut into sections, where each section shows one category's share of the total.
rules: Add the frequencies to get the total, then divide the circle into that many equal sections.
Give each category its own colour and number of sections, and draw a key.
Half the circle is 50% of the total and a quarter of the circle is 25%.

example.title: Favourite animal: elephant 1, tiger 2, giraffe 2
lines: Divide the circle into 5 equal sections
Elephant: 1 section, one fifth of the circle
Tiger: 2 sections, two fifths of the circle
Giraffe: 2 sections, two fifths of the circle

topics.title: FREQUENCY DIAGRAMS
topics.def: A frequency diagram is a bar graph for measurements, where each bar stands for an equal group of values instead of a single value.
rules: Measurements take too many different values, so sort them into equal groups first.
Choose about five groups that are all the same width and cover every measurement.
The bars sit next to each other because the groups follow on along a scale.

topics.title: LINE GRAPHS
topics.def: A line graph plots points and joins them with straight lines, usually to show how something changes over time.
rules: Plot each pair of values as a point, then join neighbouring points with straight lines.
You can read a value between two plotted points off the line, which gives an estimate.

example.title: Dee's pulse rate on a 1 hour run
lines: 40 to 50 minutes: 106 up to 130, a rise of 24
80 minutes: 68, almost back to the starting rate

topics.title: SCATTER GRAPHS
topics.def: A scatter graph plots one point for every thing that was measured twice, so you can see whether the two measurements are linked.
rules: Each point carries two measurements of the same thing, one read off each axis.
Draw the line of best fit through the middle of the points, with about as many points above it as below.
Read off the line of best fit to estimate a value you did not measure.

example.title: 11 plants: height and number of leaves
lines: The taller the plant, the more leaves it has

glossary.def: A graph that shows data as bars so that quantities are easy to compare.
glossary.example: A bar chart of rose bushes uses the groups 1-3, 4-6, 7-9, 10-12 and 13-15 roses (p.206).

glossary.def: A graph that uses one dot for each time a value or category occurs.
glossary.example: A dot plot of test marks has a column of dots above each score (p.205).

glossary.def: Information collected by observing, asking or measuring.
glossary.example: A farmer collected data on the peas found in 72 pea pods (p.207).

glossary.def: A rectangle of 100 squares divided so each colour shows a category's share of the whole.
glossary.example: The sports chosen by 20 children shown in a 100 square waffle diagram (p.207).

glossary.def: A circle divided into sections, each section showing one category's share of the total.
glossary.example: Elephant 1, tiger 2 and giraffe 2 gives a circle split into 5 equal sections (p.208).

glossary.def: A graph whose bars show groups of measurements rather than single values.
glossary.example: Jump heights grouped as 16-20, 21-25, 26-30, 31-35 and 36-40 cm (p.213).

glossary.def: A graph that joins plotted points with a line, often to show change over time.
glossary.example: Dee's pulse rate plotted every 10 minutes of a 1 hour run (p.214).

glossary.def: A graph of plotted points that shows whether two measurements are related.
glossary.example: Plant height plotted against number of leaves for 11 plants (p.218).

summary.big_en: Operations have to be carried out in a fixed order, and brackets are the way you change that order. The commutative, associative and distributive rules let you rearrange a calculation into an easier one without changing the answer.

topics.title: ORDER OF OPERATIONS
topics.def: The order of operations is the fixed order in which the parts of a calculation must be worked out.
rules: Brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.
Multiplication and division still come first even when the addition is written before them.

topics.title: BRACKETS
topics.def: Brackets are a pair of symbols placed round the part of a calculation that has to be done first.
rules: Work out everything inside the brackets before you do anything else.
Adding brackets can change the answer even though the numbers and the signs stay exactly the same.

example.title: Same numbers, different brackets
lines: Both use 3, 4, 6 and the same two signs
The brackets decide which operation is done first

topics.title: COMMUTATIVE AND ASSOCIATIVE RULES
topics.def: These two rules say that numbers which are all added, or all multiplied, give the same answer whatever order you put them in and however you group them.
rules: Commutative rule: when you add or multiply two numbers you can do the calculation in either order.
Associative rule: with more than two numbers added or multiplied you can group them in any order.
Neither rule works for subtraction or division: 8 + 5 - 7 = 6 but 8 + 7 - 5 = 10.

topics.title: DISTRIBUTIVE RULE
topics.def: The distributive rule lets you break one multiplication into two easier multiplications that are then added or subtracted.
rules: Split one of the numbers into parts, multiply each part, then put the results back together.
It works with a difference as well as a sum, which helps when a number is just below a multiple of ten.

glossary.def: The fixed order for a calculation: brackets, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.
glossary.example: 3 × 4 + 6 = 12 + 6 = 18, because the multiplication comes first (p.224).

glossary.def: A pair of symbols round the part of a calculation that must be worked out first.
When two numbers are added or multiplied, either order gives the same answer.
glossary.example: 8 + 5 - 7 = 6 but 8 + 7 - 5 = 10, so subtraction does not follow the rule (p.226).

glossary.def: When more than two numbers are added or multiplied, you may group them in any order.
One multiplication can be broken into a sum of two smaller multiplications.

summary.big_en: A transformation moves a shape without changing its size or its shape: you can slide it, flip it or turn it. Coordinates give every point an exact address on the grid, so a move can be described precisely.

topics.title: COORDINATES
topics.def: Coordinates are a pair of numbers that give the exact position of a point on a coordinate grid.
rules: Write the x-axis number first and the y-axis number second, inside brackets.
Coordinates can be negative, because the axes carry on past zero to the left and downwards.
They do not have to be whole numbers: a point can sit halfway between two lines.

branches.when: The first number is positive
branches.then: the point is to the right of zero

branches.when: The first number is negative
branches.then: the point is to the left of zero

branches.when: The second number is positive
The second number is negative

topics.title: TRANSLATIONS
topics.def: To translate a shape is to slide it a number of squares left or right and up or down, without turning it or changing its size.
rules: Move every vertex by the same amount, then join the new vertices back up.
Right adds to the x-coordinate and left subtracts; up adds to the y-coordinate and down subtracts.
The new shape is exactly the same size and the same way round as the original.

example.title: Trapezium PQRS translated 2 right and 1 up
lines: Rule: add 2 to x and add 1 to y

topics.title: REFLECTIONS
topics.def: A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line, so the image sits the same distance from the line as the original but the other way round.
rules: Take one vertex at a time: measure its distance to the mirror line and mark the same distance on the other side.
Join the new vertices with straight lines to finish the reflected shape.
A mirror line can be horizontal, vertical or diagonal, and tracing paper or a mirror helps you check.

branches.when: The mirror line is vertical
branches.then: the shape flips from left to right
branches.eg: 3 squares left of the line becomes 3 squares right

branches.when: The mirror line is horizontal
branches.then: the shape flips from top to bottom

branches.when: The mirror line is diagonal
branches.then: the shape flips across a line at 45 degrees
branches.eg: use tracing paper or a mirror to check

topics.title: ROTATIONS
topics.def: To rotate a shape is to turn it around a fixed point called the centre of rotation.
rules: A 90 degree turn is a quarter turn; clockwise goes the way a clock's hands go, anticlockwise the opposite way.
Trace the shape, hold your pencil point on the centre of rotation, then turn the tracing paper.
The turned shape stays the same size, but it is no longer facing the same way.

example.title: Rotate triangle A 90 degrees clockwise about C
lines: Step 1: trace the shape and hold your pencil on C
Step 2: turn the tracing paper a quarter turn clockwise

topics.title: CORRESPONDING VERTICES
topics.def: Corresponding vertices are the vertices that sit in the same position on a shape before and after a transformation.
rules: Vertex A on the original matches vertex A' on the image, which you say as 'A dash'.
Join corresponding vertices with straight lines to test what kind of move was used.

glossary.def: A number line drawn along the edge of a coordinate grid.
glossary.example: The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical (p.231).

glossary.def: The pair of number lines on a coordinate grid, the x-axis and the y-axis together.
glossary.example: Draw axes from -5 to +5 on squared paper (p.233).

glossary.def: To move a shape a number of squares left or right and up or down.
glossary.example: Translate trapezium PQRS 2 squares right and 1 square up (p.233).

glossary.def: A point corresponds to another when it sits in the same place on the shape before and after a move.
glossary.example: Vertex A corresponds with vertex A' on the translated triangle (p.231).

glossary.def: A mirror line drawn at 45 degrees to a horizontal or a vertical line.
glossary.example: Reflect the trapezium in the diagonal mirror line (p.238).

glossary.def: To turn a shape around a fixed point.
glossary.example: Rotate triangle A 90 degrees clockwise about centre C (p.242).

glossary.def: The fixed point that a shape is turned about.
glossary.example: The centre of rotation is marked with the letter C on the grid (p.242).

flashcards.front_en: Name the three places after the decimal point.
flashcards.back_en: Tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

flashcards.front_en: What happens to the digits when you multiply by 1000?
flashcards.back_en: Every digit moves three places to the left.

flashcards.front_en: What happens to the digits when you divide by 100?
flashcards.back_en: Every digit moves two places to the right.

flashcards.front_en: Rounding to the nearest tenth: which digit do you look at?
flashcards.back_en: The hundredths digit. 0–4 rounds down, 5–9 rounds up.

flashcards.front_en: Rounding to the nearest whole number: which digit do you look at?
flashcards.back_en: The tenths digit, using the same 0–4 down, 5–9 up rule.

flashcards.front_en: What does it mean to regroup a number?
flashcards.back_en: Write the same number as a different set of parts, with the same total.

flashcards.front_en: How do you read the digits after a decimal point?
flashcards.back_en: One by one: 2.139 is two point one three nine.

flashcards.front_en: What does a position-to-term rule do?
flashcards.back_en: Gives any term straight from its position, without listing them all.

flashcards.front_en: What is the ninth square number?
flashcards.back_en: 81, because 9 × 9 = 81.
A number that divides exactly into both numbers.
One of the symbols 0 to 9 that a number is written with.
flashcards.example_en: The digit 7 in 213.807 stands for 7 thousandths (p.13).

flashcards.back_en: The value a digit has because of its position in the number.
flashcards.example_en: In 6703.46 the 7 has a place value of 7 hundreds (p.13).

flashcards.back_en: The dot that separates the whole-number part from the part smaller than one.
The first place after the decimal point.
flashcards.example_en: In 13.136 the 1 after the point is 1 tenth (p.13).

flashcards.back_en: The second place after the decimal point.
The third place after the decimal point.
Putting parts together to make a number.
Splitting a number into the parts it is made of.
Writing the same number as a different set of parts.
flashcards.example_en: 56.079 is also 56 ones and 79 thousandths (WB p.9).

flashcards.back_en: Replace a number with a nearby number that is easier to use.
The closest of the possible answers.
A number written with a decimal point, so it can show parts smaller than one.
One of the numbers in a sequence.
Where a term sits in the sequence: first, second, third and so on.
A rule that takes you from one term to the next.
A rule that gives the term from its position.
flashcards.example_en: Multiply the position by 2, so the 50th term is 100 (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: The result of multiplying a number by itself.
The result of multiplying a number by itself three times.
A number in another number's times table.
A number that divides into another number exactly.
A multiple that two or more numbers share.
flashcards.example_en: 24 is a common multiple of 3 and 8 (p.30).

flashcards.back_en: A factor that two or more numbers share.
flashcards.example_en: The common factors of 18 and 24 are 1, 2, 3 and 6 (p.32).

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the mean?
flashcards.back_en: Add all the values, then divide by how many there are.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the median?
flashcards.back_en: Put the values in order and take the middle one.
The value that appears most often. Two modes means bimodal.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the range?
flashcards.back_en: Largest value minus smallest value.
A whole number, positive, negative or zero.

flashcards.front_en: What is the difference between −6 and 4?
flashcards.back_en: 10 — six steps up to zero, then four more.

flashcards.front_en: Is x − 3 the same as 3 − x?
flashcards.back_en: No. Addition can be swapped round, subtraction cannot.
A constant always stays the same; a variable can change.
One number that represents a whole set of data.
flashcards.example_en: A book scored an average of 6 out of 10 by its reviewers (p.39).

flashcards.back_en: The value that appears most often.
Having two modes.
The middle value when the data is put in order.
The total of the values divided by how many there are.
The difference between the largest and smallest value.
A whole number, which can be positive, negative or zero.
A number greater than zero.
flashcards.example_en: A depth of 550 m below the surface (p.49).

flashcards.back_en: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign.
How far apart two numbers are.
flashcards.example_en: The difference in temperature between two cities (p.51).

flashcards.back_en: A value that always stays the same.
A letter standing for a value that can change.
flashcards.example_en: d is the dice score, so it changes each throw (p.55).

flashcards.back_en: A rough answer worked out by rounding the numbers first.
A rule written with numbers and letters, such as d + 4.
flashcards.example_en: When the dice score d is 5, d + 4 is 9 (p.55).

flashcards.front_en: When you round to the nearest tenth, how many digits come after the decimal point?
flashcards.back_en: One digit, and you keep it even when that digit is 0: 3.95 rounds to 4.0, not 4.

flashcards.front_en: What four things describe a quadrilateral?
flashcards.back_en: Its sides, its angles, its diagonals and its lines of symmetry.

flashcards.front_en: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have?
flashcards.back_en: Two: one horizontal and one vertical.
Square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, isosceles trapezium, rhombus and kite.

flashcards.front_en: What angle do the diagonals of a square meet at?
flashcards.back_en: 90 degrees, and they also bisect each other.

flashcards.front_en: How is the diameter related to the radius?
flashcards.back_en: The diameter is twice the radius, so a radius of 3 cm gives a diameter of 6 cm.

flashcards.front_en: How do you draw a circle of radius 5 cm?
flashcards.back_en: Open the compasses to 5 cm, put the point on the centre dot and turn them right round.

flashcards.front_en: Two circles touch. How far apart are their centres?
flashcards.back_en: The two radii added together, so 6 cm and 2.5 cm gives 8.5 cm.

flashcards.front_en: What is the smallest possible order of rotational symmetry?
flashcards.back_en: One, because every shape looks the same again after one full turn.

flashcards.front_en: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a square?
flashcards.back_en: Four, because it looks the same in four positions in one full turn.

flashcards.front_en: What does the fraction 7/4 mean as a division?
flashcards.back_en: 7 divided by 4, which is one whole and three quarters, or 1 3/4.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find 3/4 of an amount?
flashcards.back_en: Divide the amount by 4, then multiply that result by 3.

flashcards.front_en: Does 4/3 of 12 give more or less than 12?
flashcards.back_en: More. An improper fraction is bigger than one whole, so 4/3 of 12 is 16.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find 10% of a quantity?
flashcards.back_en: Divide it by 10, because 10% is the same as 1/10. 10% of 40 is 4.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find 20% of a quantity?
flashcards.back_en: Find 10% by dividing by 10, then multiply that answer by 2.

flashcards.front_en: Why can you not find 50% by dividing by 5?
flashcards.back_en: 50% is a half, so you divide by 2. Dividing by 5 gives 20%.

flashcards.front_en: How do you simplify a fraction?
flashcards.back_en: Divide the numerator and denominator by the same number, repeating until you cannot go any further.

flashcards.front_en: How do you turn a fraction with denominator 100 into a percentage?
flashcards.back_en: The numerator is the percentage, so 57/100 is 57%.

flashcards.front_en: How do you order fractions, decimals and percentages?
flashcards.back_en: Change them all into the same form first, then compare and put them in order.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the area of a rectangle?
flashcards.back_en: Multiply the length by the width, then write the answer in square units such as cm² or m².

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the area of a triangle?
flashcards.back_en: Work out the area of the rectangle it is half of, then divide that area by 2.

flashcards.front_en: How do you work back from a triangle to its rectangle?
flashcards.back_en: Double the area of the triangle. A triangle of 9 cm² came from a rectangle of 18 cm².

flashcards.front_en: How do you count part-covered squares?
flashcards.back_en: Count a square that is about half covered as half a square, and put the other part squares together to make whole ones.

flashcards.front_en: Which units are used for area?
flashcards.back_en: Square units: mm², cm², m² and km².

flashcards.front_en: How many minutes is 0.1 of an hour?
flashcards.back_en: 6 minutes, because 60 ÷ 10 = 6. So 0.7 of an hour is 7 × 6 = 42 minutes.

flashcards.front_en: How do you change decimal hours into hours and minutes?
flashcards.back_en: Keep the whole hours, then multiply the part after the point by 60 to get the minutes.

flashcards.front_en: Why is 1.25 hours not 1 hour and 25 minutes?
flashcards.back_en: The figures after the point are parts of an hour, not minutes. 0.25 of an hour is 15 minutes.

flashcards.front_en: How do you change decimal minutes into minutes and seconds?
flashcards.back_en: Multiply the part after the point by 60. In 159.1 minutes, 0.1 of a minute is 6 seconds.
They give both numbers the same number of decimal places so the columns match. Write 10 as 10.00.

flashcards.front_en: What should you do before adding decimals?
flashcards.back_en: Make an estimate, then check the answer against it to see whether the result is sensible.
0.7 is the same as 0.70, so 0.70 + 0.41 = 1.11. Line up the points, not the last digits.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find a common denominator?
flashcards.back_en: List the multiples of both denominators and pick a number in both lists. For 5 and 4 that is 20.

flashcards.front_en: What are the steps for adding two fractions?
flashcards.back_en: Find a common denominator, write equivalent fractions, add the numerators, then simplify and change improper fractions to mixed numbers.

flashcards.front_en: When you add fractions, what do you NOT add?
flashcards.back_en: The denominators. Once both fractions have the same denominator, only the numerators are added.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find a missing part of a whole?
flashcards.back_en: Add the parts you know, then subtract that total from the whole. 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so 7/12 is left.
Yes. 15/15 makes one whole and 4/15 is left over, so the two answers are equal.

flashcards.front_en: How can you write a probability?
flashcards.back_en: As a fraction or as a percentage. 5 out of 10 cards is 5/10, which is 50%.

flashcards.front_en: What is the probability of something certain?
flashcards.back_en: It happens for every outcome, so it is 10 out of 10, or 100%.

flashcards.front_en: How do you test if two events are mutually exclusive?
flashcards.back_en: Look for one outcome that fits both events. If there is none, the events are mutually exclusive.

flashcards.front_en: Are odd numbers and multiples of 10 mutually exclusive?
flashcards.back_en: For tickets 1 to 30, yes. The multiples of 10 are 10, 20 and 30, and none of them is odd.

flashcards.front_en: How do you predict results for more spins?
flashcards.back_en: Keep the same fraction of the trials. Red 4 times in 8 spins means red 20 times in 40 spins.

flashcards.front_en: 10 objects, 3 blue, 20 turns. How many blue?
flashcards.back_en: About 6, because blue is 3 out of every 10 objects and 3 out of 10 of 20 is 6.

flashcards.front_en: How do you work out an experimental probability?
flashcards.back_en: Count how many times the outcome happened out of the total number of trials, such as 16 out of 40.

flashcards.front_en: Why carry out more trials in an experiment?
flashcards.back_en: A large number of trials shows the likelihood of an event much better than a small number does.
So you can check that the real answer is a sensible size and spot a big mistake.

flashcards.front_en: How do you check a multiplication?
flashcards.back_en: Use the inverse operation: divide the answer by one of the numbers you multiplied.

flashcards.front_en: How do you multiply a number by 30?
flashcards.back_en: Multiply by 3, then multiply that answer by 10.

flashcards.front_en: How do you multiply by a 2-digit number?
flashcards.back_en: Split it into tens and ones, multiply by each part, then add the two answers.

flashcards.front_en: What is the first step in a long division?
flashcards.back_en: Estimate the answer by rounding the dividend and the divisor.

flashcards.front_en: How can factors make a division easier?
flashcards.back_en: Divide by one factor of the divisor, then divide that answer by the other factor.

flashcards.front_en: Two ways to write the leftover in a division?
flashcards.back_en: After an r as a whole number, or as a fraction with the divisor underneath.

flashcards.front_en: State the divisibility tests for 3, 6 and 9.
flashcards.back_en: 3: digit sum is a multiple of 3. 9: digit sum is a multiple of 9. 6: even and divisible by 3.

flashcards.front_en: How do you describe a compound 3D shape?
flashcards.back_en: Name the simple shapes it splits into; more than one answer can be right.
flashcards.example_en: A cube and a cuboid, or two cuboids (p.149)

flashcards.front_en: How many faces does a triangular prism have?
flashcards.back_en: Five: two triangles and three rectangles.

flashcards.front_en: How many faces does a square based pyramid have?
flashcards.back_en: Five: one square and four triangles.

flashcards.front_en: Does each 3D shape have only one net?
flashcards.back_en: No. Most shapes have several different nets that all fold up correctly.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the surface area of a cuboid?
flashcards.back_en: Work out the area of each of the six faces, then add them together.

flashcards.front_en: What is the difference between capacity and volume?
flashcards.back_en: Capacity is the most a container can hold; volume is how much is in it now.
flashcards.example_en: A 600 ml jug holding 500 ml of water (p.154)

flashcards.front_en: How do you write 2500 ml in litres?
flashcards.back_en: 2 litres 500 ml, or 2.5 litres, because 1 litre is 1000 ml.

flashcards.front_en: How do you estimate the volume in a container?
flashcards.back_en: Judge what fraction of the container is full, then work out that fraction of its capacity.

flashcards.front_en: Which compares part to part: ratio or proportion?
flashcards.back_en: Ratio compares part with part. Proportion compares a part with the whole.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find a missing number in an equivalent ratio?
flashcards.back_en: Work out what the known part was multiplied by, then multiply the other part by the same number.

flashcards.front_en: How do you write a ratio in its simplest form?
flashcards.back_en: Divide both parts by the largest number that goes into both of them.

flashcards.front_en: Name three ways of writing a proportion.
flashcards.back_en: As 'x in every y', as a fraction, or as a percentage.

flashcards.front_en: What stays the same in direct proportion?
flashcards.back_en: The ratio between the two quantities stays the same as they grow or shrink.

flashcards.front_en: What does a scale of 1 : 24 mean?
flashcards.back_en: Every length on the real object is 24 times the matching length on the model.
flashcards.example_en: 170 mm model gives a 4080 mm real car (p.172)

flashcards.front_en: How do you change a recipe for 8 people to 4?
flashcards.back_en: Halve every ingredient, because 4 is half of 8.

flashcards.front_en: What happens to the angles when a shape is enlarged?
flashcards.back_en: They stay exactly the same size; only the lengths change, all in the same ratio.

flashcards.front_en: Which ring of protractor numbers should you read?
flashcards.back_en: The outside ring when the angle opens clockwise from 0°, the inside ring when it opens anticlockwise.

flashcards.front_en: Two things to line up before reading an angle
flashcards.back_en: The centre of the protractor on the point of the angle, and one arm exactly on 0°.

flashcards.front_en: Steps for drawing an angle of a given size
flashcards.back_en: Draw a line, mark the size with the protractor, join the mark to the line, then label the angle.

flashcards.front_en: What do the angles in a triangle add up to?
flashcards.back_en: They always add up to 180°, whatever the size or shape of the triangle.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find a missing angle in a triangle?
flashcards.back_en: Add the angles you already know, then subtract that total from 180°.
All three angles are equal, so each one is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
Two angles are equal; the dashes on two sides show which sides, and so which angles, match.
Angles that meet at a point on a straight line add up to 180°.

flashcards.front_en: Two angle facts worth learning by heart
flashcards.back_en: A right angle is 90°, shown by a small square, and a full turn is 360°.

flashcards.front_en: How do you multiply a fraction by a whole number?
flashcards.back_en: Multiply the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same.

flashcards.front_en: When is the answer to a fraction multiplication more than 1?
flashcards.back_en: When the new numerator becomes bigger than the denominator, giving an improper fraction.

flashcards.front_en: How do you divide a fraction by a whole number?
flashcards.back_en: Multiply the denominator by the whole number, keep the numerator, then simplify the answer.

flashcards.front_en: Two ways to tidy up a fraction answer
flashcards.back_en: Write an improper fraction as a mixed number, and reduce the fraction to its simplest form.

flashcards.front_en: What do you do before multiplying decimals?
flashcards.back_en: Estimate by rounding both numbers, then check that the real answer is close to the estimate.

flashcards.front_en: Multiplying a decimal by a 2-digit whole number
flashcards.back_en: Multiply by the ones, then by the tens, and add the two answers together.

flashcards.front_en: How do you divide a decimal by a whole number?
flashcards.back_en: Estimate, then take away multiples of the divisor, working down from the ones to the tenths.

flashcards.front_en: How can you check a division answer?
flashcards.back_en: Multiply the quotient by the divisor and you should get the dividend back.

flashcards.front_en: What does one dot mean on a dot plot?
flashcards.back_en: One item with that value. The height of the column is the frequency.

flashcards.front_en: How do you find the total from a bar chart?
flashcards.back_en: Add together the frequency of every single bar.

flashcards.front_en: What does one square mean on a 100 square waffle?
flashcards.back_en: One per cent of the whole set of data.

flashcards.front_en: A 100 square waffle shows 20 children. Squares each?
flashcards.back_en: 100 divided by 20 is 5 squares for each child, which is 5%.

flashcards.front_en: How do you start a pie chart from a frequency table?
flashcards.back_en: Add the frequencies to get the total, then split the circle into that many equal sections.

flashcards.front_en: Why does a frequency diagram use groups?
