flashcards.back_en: Measurements take too many different values, so equal groups keep the diagram readable.

flashcards.front_en: What is a line graph best for?
flashcards.back_en: Showing how something changes over time, such as temperature or pulse rate.

flashcards.front_en: Where should a line of best fit go?
flashcards.back_en: Through the middle of the points, with about as many points above it as below.

flashcards.front_en: How do you estimate a missing value on a scatter graph?
flashcards.back_en: Go from the known measurement to the line of best fit, then read off the other axis.

flashcards.front_en: What is the order of operations?
flashcards.back_en: Brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

flashcards.front_en: In 6 + 3 × 4, which part do you do first?
flashcards.back_en: The multiplication: 3 × 4 = 12, and then 6 + 12 = 18.

flashcards.front_en: Why can brackets change an answer?
flashcards.back_en: They force the operation inside them to be done first, ahead of the usual order.

flashcards.front_en: Which operations can be reordered freely?
flashcards.back_en: Only addition and multiplication. Subtraction cannot: 8 + 5 - 7 = 6 but 8 + 7 - 5 = 10.

flashcards.front_en: What does the associative rule let you do?
flashcards.back_en: Group numbers that are all added or all multiplied any way you like: 42 × 24 = 42 × 2 × 12.

flashcards.front_en: How do you use the distributive rule on 3 × 67?
flashcards.back_en: Split 67 into 60 + 7, then add 180 and 21 to get 201.

flashcards.front_en: In coordinates, which axis number is written first?
flashcards.back_en: The x-axis number, and then the y-axis number, like this: (x, y).

flashcards.front_en: What does a negative x-coordinate tell you?
flashcards.back_en: The point is left of zero. A negative y-coordinate means it is below zero.

flashcards.front_en: How do you translate a shape on a grid?
flashcards.back_en: Move every vertex the same number of squares across and up or down, then join them.

flashcards.front_en: What happens to coordinates in a translation left and down?
flashcards.back_en: Subtract from the x-coordinate for left, and subtract from the y-coordinate for down.

flashcards.front_en: How do you reflect a shape in a mirror line?
flashcards.back_en: Mark each vertex the same distance the other side of the line, then join the vertices.

flashcards.front_en: What are the four steps for rotating a shape?
flashcards.back_en: Trace it, hold your pencil on the centre, turn a quarter turn, then draw and label it.
The same way as the hands of a clock. Anticlockwise goes the opposite way.

flashcards.front_en: What do lines joining corresponding vertices look like?
flashcards.back_en: Parallel after a translation or a reflection, but never parallel after a rotation.
Cut exactly in half.
flashcards.example_en: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other (p.64).

flashcards.back_en: A line that joins opposite corners of a quadrilateral.
flashcards.example_en: The two diagonals of a square meet at 90 degrees (p.65).

flashcards.back_en: Lines that never meet and always stay the same distance apart.
flashcards.example_en: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides (p.65).

flashcards.back_en: Give a reason for your answer.
flashcards.example_en: Side a is parallel to g because both are parallel to e (p.68).

flashcards.back_en: The plural of trapezium.
flashcards.example_en: Trapezia can be sorted into those that are isosceles and those that are not (p.66).

flashcards.back_en: The middle point of a circle.
flashcards.example_en: Put the point of the compasses on the centre before you turn them (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: The perimeter of a circle, the distance all the way round it.
flashcards.example_en: A diameter joins two points on the circumference (p.70).

flashcards.back_en: A line joining the centre of a circle to the circumference.
flashcards.example_en: Arun draws a circle with a radius of 3 cm (p.73).

flashcards.back_en: A line joining two points on the circumference that passes through the centre.
flashcards.example_en: A circle with a diameter of 60 mm has a radius of 3 cm (p.73).

flashcards.back_en: An instrument used to draw circles.
flashcards.example_en: Open your compasses to 4 cm to draw a circle of radius 4 cm (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: When a shape can be turned about a point to a new position and still look the same.
flashcards.example_en: A rectangle has rotational symmetry of order 2 (p.76).

flashcards.back_en: The number of times a shape looks the same in one full turn.
flashcards.example_en: A button made of four identical parts has order 4 (p.76).

flashcards.back_en: The top number of a fraction.
The bottom number of a fraction, showing how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
A fraction smaller than one whole, where the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
A fraction equal to or greater than one whole, where the numerator is at least as big as the denominator.
A whole number and a proper fraction written together.
flashcards.example_en: 7/4 is the same as the mixed number 1 3/4 (p.85).

flashcards.back_en: A fraction used to find that fraction of an amount.
flashcards.example_en: Finding 6/5 of a number uses the fraction as an operator (p.86).

flashcards.back_en: The number of parts out of every hundred.
flashcards.example_en: 10% off a jumper costing $20 takes $2 off the price (p.88).

flashcards.back_en: An amount written as a number of parts per hundred, using the % sign.
flashcards.example_en: A shop offers 25% off in its sale (p.88).

flashcards.back_en: Reduce the numerator and the denominator of a fraction to smaller numbers.
A fraction whose numerator and denominator cannot be reduced any further.
A fraction that has exactly the same value as another fraction.
flashcards.example_en: 6/10 and 60/100 are equivalent fractions, both equal to 0.6 (p.94).

flashcards.back_en: The size of the surface a shape covers, measured in square units such as cm² and m².
flashcards.example_en: A rectangle 8 m by 4 m has an area of 32 m² (p.104).

flashcards.back_en: A unit of area the size of a square measuring 1 cm by 1 cm, written cm².
flashcards.example_en: The triangles are drawn on a centimetre square grid, so each square is 1 cm² (p.102).

flashcards.back_en: A length of time from a starting point to an ending point.
flashcards.example_en: 3.7 hours is a time interval written as a decimal (p.107).

flashcards.back_en: A time written with more than one unit together, such as hours and minutes.
flashcards.example_en: 3.7 hours in mixed units is 3 hours and 42 minutes (p.107).

flashcards.back_en: The position of a digit to the right of the decimal point.
A zero written at the end of a decimal so that two numbers have the same number of decimal places.
A number that both denominators divide into, so two fractions can be written with parts of the same size.
flashcards.example_en: 20 is a common denominator for 9/5 and 3/4 (p.118).

flashcards.back_en: Fractions that are worth the same amount, even though they are written differently.
A number that shows the chance of an event happening.
flashcards.example_en: The probability of taking a 2 from ten cards is 1/10, or 10% (p.125).

flashcards.back_en: Outcomes that have the same probability as each other.
flashcards.example_en: A coin is equally likely to land heads up or tails up (p.122).

flashcards.back_en: One or more outcomes grouped together and described in one sentence.
flashcards.example_en: 'The spinner lands on a number less than 6' is an event (p.131).

flashcards.back_en: Events that cannot happen at the same time.
flashcards.example_en: Spinning a 5 and spinning a number less than 4 are mutually exclusive (p.126).

flashcards.back_en: How likely an event is to happen, from impossible up to certain.
flashcards.example_en: Asubi uses likelihood to predict that a spinner lands on red 4 times in 8 spins (p.129).

flashcards.back_en: The result of one trial in a probability experiment.
flashcards.example_en: Heads up and tails up are the two outcomes of flipping a coin (p.125).

flashcards.back_en: A situation where a number of trials are carried out to explore probability.
flashcards.example_en: Keran flipped a coin 40 times and recorded the results in a tally chart (p.125).

flashcards.back_en: The answer you get when numbers are multiplied together.
The number that is being divided.
The number you are dividing by.
The answer to a division.
The amount left over when a number does not divide exactly.
A number is divisible by another when it divides exactly, with nothing left over.
A quick rule for deciding whether a number divides exactly, without doing the division.
flashcards.example_en: A number is divisible by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3 (p.142).

flashcards.back_en: Overlapping circles used to sort numbers into groups, with numbers in both groups in the overlap.
flashcards.example_en: 24 goes in the overlap of 'divisible by 3' and 'divisible by 6' (p.143).

flashcards.back_en: The operation that undoes another one.
A shape made up of two or more simpler shapes joined together.
flashcards.example_en: A cube joined to a cuboid makes a compound shape (p.149).

flashcards.back_en: A flat pattern of joined faces that folds up to make a 3D shape.
flashcards.example_en: The net of a cuboid has four rectangles and two squares (p.150).

flashcards.back_en: A 3D shape with two identical parallel faces, with rectangles for all the other faces.
flashcards.example_en: A triangular prism has 2 triangular faces and 3 rectangular faces (p.151).

flashcards.back_en: The total area of all the faces of a 3D shape.
flashcards.example_en: The surface area of a cuboid is the area of its six faces added together (p.151).

flashcards.back_en: The greatest amount that a container can hold.
flashcards.example_en: A jug marked up to 600 ml has a capacity of 600 ml (p.154).

flashcards.back_en: The amount of space taken up by an object, liquid or gas.
flashcards.example_en: Water standing at the 500 ml mark has a volume of 500 ml (p.154).

flashcards.back_en: A unit used to measure capacity and volume; one litre is 1000 millilitres.
flashcards.example_en: 2500 ml is the same as 2.5 litres (p.155).

flashcards.back_en: A comparison between two or more quantities that compares part with part.
flashcards.example_en: A bowl of 6 apples and 3 oranges gives the ratio 6 : 3 (p.166).

flashcards.back_en: A ratio that means the same as another, made by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number.
flashcards.example_en: 3 : 5 = 27 : 45, because both parts are multiplied by 9 (p.166).

flashcards.back_en: A part compared with the whole, telling you how many out of the total.
flashcards.example_en: In green paint made from 2 cans of blue and 3 of yellow, 2 in every 5 cans are blue (p.164).

flashcards.back_en: The relationship between two quantities whose ratio stays the same, so when one increases the other increases too.
flashcards.example_en: 1 hour of work earns $20, 2 hours earn $40 and 4 hours earn $80 (p.165).

flashcards.back_en: To make a shape bigger or smaller so that every length changes in the same ratio.
flashcards.example_en: A 5 cm by 2 cm rectangle enlarged in the ratio 1 : 2 becomes 10 cm by 4 cm (p.172).

flashcards.back_en: A ratio that compares the size of a model with the size of the real object.
flashcards.example_en: A scale of 1 : 24 means the real car is 24 times as long as the model (p.172).

flashcards.back_en: An instrument used for measuring and drawing angles.
flashcards.example_en: A protractor is marked from 0° to 360° around its edge (p.178).

flashcards.back_en: Turning in the same direction as the hands of a clock.
flashcards.example_en: An angle that opens clockwise from 0° is read on the outside numbers (p.178).

flashcards.back_en: Turning in the opposite direction to the hands of a clock.
flashcards.example_en: An angle that opens anticlockwise from 0° is read on the inside numbers (p.178).

flashcards.back_en: The small curved line drawn between two arms to show which angle is meant.
flashcards.example_en: After drawing 120° you add an arc and write the size on it (p.179).

flashcards.back_en: A triangle whose three sides are all different lengths and whose three angles are all different sizes.
flashcards.example_en: A triangle with angles 35°, 45° and 100° is scalene (p.186).

flashcards.back_en: A triangle with two sides equal in length and two angles equal in size.
flashcards.example_en: An isosceles triangle with angles of 50° and 50° has a third angle of 80° (p.185).

flashcards.back_en: A triangle with all three sides equal in length and all three angles equal in size.
flashcards.example_en: Each angle in an equilateral triangle is 60° (p.186).

flashcards.back_en: An angle of exactly 90°, marked on a diagram with a small square symbol.
flashcards.example_en: A right-angled triangle with a 28° angle has a third angle of 62° (p.185).

flashcards.back_en: A graph that shows data as bars so that quantities are easy to compare.
flashcards.example_en: A bar chart of rose bushes uses the groups 1-3, 4-6, 7-9, 10-12 and 13-15 roses (p.206).

flashcards.back_en: A graph that uses one dot for each time a value or category occurs.
flashcards.example_en: A dot plot of test marks has a column of dots above each score (p.205).

flashcards.back_en: Information collected by observing, asking or measuring.
flashcards.example_en: A farmer collected data on the peas found in 72 pea pods (p.207).

flashcards.back_en: A rectangle of 100 squares divided so each colour shows a category's share of the whole.
flashcards.example_en: The sports chosen by 20 children shown in a 100 square waffle diagram (p.207).

flashcards.back_en: A circle divided into sections, each section showing one category's share of the total.
flashcards.example_en: Elephant 1, tiger 2 and giraffe 2 gives a circle split into 5 equal sections (p.208).

flashcards.back_en: A graph whose bars show groups of measurements rather than single values.
flashcards.example_en: Jump heights grouped as 16-20, 21-25, 26-30, 31-35 and 36-40 cm (p.213).

flashcards.back_en: A graph that joins plotted points with a line, often to show change over time.
flashcards.example_en: Dee's pulse rate plotted every 10 minutes of a 1 hour run (p.214).

flashcards.back_en: A graph of plotted points that shows whether two measurements are related.
flashcards.example_en: Plant height plotted against number of leaves for 11 plants (p.218).

flashcards.back_en: The fixed order for a calculation: brackets, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.
A pair of symbols round the part of a calculation that must be worked out first.
When two numbers are added or multiplied, either order gives the same answer.
flashcards.example_en: 8 + 5 - 7 = 6 but 8 + 7 - 5 = 10, so subtraction does not follow the rule (p.226).

flashcards.back_en: When more than two numbers are added or multiplied, you may group them in any order.
One multiplication can be broken into a sum of two smaller multiplications.
A number line drawn along the edge of a coordinate grid.
flashcards.example_en: The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical (p.231).

flashcards.back_en: The pair of number lines on a coordinate grid, the x-axis and the y-axis together.
flashcards.example_en: Draw axes from -5 to +5 on squared paper (p.233).

flashcards.back_en: To move a shape a number of squares left or right and up or down.
flashcards.example_en: Translate trapezium PQRS 2 squares right and 1 square up (p.233).

flashcards.back_en: A point corresponds to another when it sits in the same place on the shape before and after a move.
flashcards.example_en: Vertex A corresponds with vertex A' on the translated triangle (p.231).

flashcards.back_en: A mirror line drawn at 45 degrees to a horizontal or a vertical line.
flashcards.example_en: Reflect the trapezium in the diagonal mirror line (p.238).

flashcards.back_en: To turn a shape around a fixed point.
flashcards.example_en: Rotate triangle A 90 degrees clockwise about centre C (p.242).

flashcards.back_en: The fixed point that a shape is turned about.
flashcards.example_en: The centre of rotation is marked with the letter C on the grid (p.242).

flashcards.back_en: A triangle with one angle of 90°.
flashcards.example_en: Cutting a rectangle along its diagonal makes two right-angled triangles (p.103).

flashcards.back_en: Fractions that already share the same denominator, so they can be added straight away.
A ratio written with the smallest whole numbers possible.
Adding the same number again and again, which is what multiplying by a whole number means.
A fraction with 1 on top, such as 1/4.
flashcards.example_en: Dividing by a whole number splits a fraction into unit fractions (p.195).

flashcards.back_en: One part of a multiplication that is worked out on its own before the parts are added.
flashcards.example_en: For 4 × 3.2, work out 4 × 3 and 4 × 0.2, then add (p.197).

flashcards.back_en: Dividing by writing the calculation out in one line with the remainders carried across.
Divide the top and the bottom of a fraction by the same number to make it simpler.

quiz.stem_en: What is the value of the digit 7 in 6703.46?
quiz.why_en: The 7 sits in the hundreds column (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What is the value of the digit 7 in 213.807?
quiz.why_en: It is the third place after the decimal point (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What is the value of the digit 7 in 456.702?
quiz.why_en: It is the first place after the decimal point (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What does the digit 5 in 3.065 represent?
quiz.why_en: It is the third place after the decimal point (WB p.9).

quiz.stem_en: How many times bigger is the value of the digit 6 in 64.53 than the value of the digit 6 in 0.367?
quiz.why_en: 6 tens against 6 hundredths is three places, so 1000 times (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: In the number 13.136, which digit is in the hundredths place?
quiz.why_en: Hundredths is the second place after the decimal point (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What is 5.6 × 100?
quiz.why_en: Every digit moves two places to the left (WB p.11).
Every digit moves three places to the left (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: What is 670 ÷ 1000?
quiz.why_en: Every digit moves three places to the right (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: What is 191 ÷ 100?
quiz.why_en: Every digit moves two places to the right (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: Find the missing number: ___ × 0.9 = 9
quiz.why_en: 0.9 must move one place to the left, so multiply by 10 (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: Find the missing number: 705 ÷ ___ = 7.05
quiz.why_en: The digits move two places to the right, so divide by 100 (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: A number is multiplied by 10, then by 10 again, then by 10 again, and the answer is 7. What was the starting number?
quiz.why_en: Three multiplications by 10 is × 1000, so reverse it: 7 ÷ 1000 (WB p.12).

quiz.stem_en: Write 10 + 3 + 1 tenth + 3 hundredths + 6 thousandths as a decimal number.
quiz.why_en: Each part goes in its own place value column (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: Copy and complete: 87.655 = 80 + 7 + ___
quiz.why_en: The decimal part decomposes into 6 tenths, 5 hundredths and 5 thousandths (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: What decimal number is 90 + 7 + 3 tenths + 1 hundredth + 4 thousandths?
quiz.why_en: Put each part in its place value column (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: Magda regroups 56.079. Which of these is NOT the same number?
quiz.why_en: 56 + 0.79 is 56.79, which is ten times bigger in the decimal part (WB p.9).

quiz.stem_en: Which expression is equal to 4.063?
quiz.why_en: 6 is in the hundredths place and 3 in the thousandths place (WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: Why do we round numbers?

choices.en: To make them easier to describe and understand

quiz.why_en: Rounding makes numbers easier to describe and understand (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 4.09 rounded to the nearest whole number?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 0, so round down (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 7.45 rounded to the nearest whole number?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 4, which is in 0–4, so round down (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: A book costs $14.65. What is that to the nearest dollar?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 6, so round up (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 9.55 rounded to the nearest whole number?
quiz.why_en: The tenths digit is 5, so round up from 9 to 10 (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: What is 8.80 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit is 0, so round down (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 3.95 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit 5 rounds the tenths digit up from 9, carrying into the ones (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: What is 3.08 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit is 8, so round up (p.19).

quiz.stem_en: What is 9.07 rounded to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: The hundredths digit is 7, so round up (p.17).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these rounds to 7.5 to the nearest tenth?
quiz.why_en: 7.49 has hundredths digit 9, so the 4 tenths round up to 5 (p.17).

quiz.stem_en: How do you write 2.139 in words?

choices.en: Two point one hundred and thirty-nine

quiz.why_en: After the decimal point the digits are said one by one (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: Which number is 'twenty point four three one'?
quiz.why_en: Twenty, then the digits 4, 3, 1 after the point (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: How do you write 0.375 in words?
quiz.why_en: The digits after the point are read separately (p.12, p.14).

quiz.stem_en: A sequence starts at 2 and the rule is add 3. What are the next three terms?
quiz.why_en: Add 3 each time: 2, 5, 8, 11 (p.22).

quiz.stem_en: The first term is 4 and the term-to-term rule is add 7. What is the fourth term?
A sequence counts back in steps of 0.2 from 1. What comes after 0.6?
quiz.why_en: Each step subtracts 0.2 (p.22).

quiz.stem_en: A sequence has terms 2, 4, 6, 8. What is the position-to-term rule?
quiz.why_en: Position 1 gives 2, position 2 gives 4, so multiply by 2 (p.23).

quiz.stem_en: With the position-to-term rule 'multiply by 2', what is the 50th term?
With the position-to-term rule 'multiply by 4', what is the 25th term?
What is the difference between a term-to-term rule and a position-to-term rule?

choices.en: They are two names for the same thing
Term-to-term only works for even numbers
Position-to-term only works for the first ten terms
Term-to-term gives the next term; position-to-term gives any term straight away

quiz.why_en: The position-to-term rule lets you find any term without writing them all out (p.22).

quiz.stem_en: What is the ninth square number?
What is 7²?
What does the small 2 in 5² mean?
quiz.why_en: The notation 2 means squared (p.27).

quiz.stem_en: Which two square numbers add up to 45?
What is 5³?
What is 3³?
Which is larger, 2³ or 3²?
Which two cube numbers add up to 152?
Which number is a multiple of both 3 and 5 and less than 20?
quiz.why_en: 15 is in both the 3 and 5 times tables (p.30).

quiz.stem_en: What are the factors of 18?
quiz.why_en: These are the numbers that divide 18 exactly (p.32).

quiz.stem_en: What are the common factors of 18 and 24?
quiz.why_en: They are the factors that appear in both lists (p.32).

quiz.stem_en: Which numbers are factors of both 30 and 20?
quiz.why_en: These divide both 30 and 20 exactly (p.32).

quiz.stem_en: All the common multiples of 3 and 8 that are less than 50 are:
quiz.why_en: 24 and 48 are in both times tables and below 50 (p.32).

quiz.stem_en: Two sequences go 3, 6, 9, 12 … and 5, 10, 15, 20 … Which number over 100 is in both?
quiz.why_en: 105 is a multiple of both 3 and 5 (p.32).

quiz.stem_en: What is the mode of 4 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm?
quiz.why_en: Both 4 and 5 appear twice, so the set is bimodal (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: What is the mode of 4, 7, 5, 4, 10?
quiz.why_en: 4 is the only value that appears more than once (p.45).

quiz.stem_en: A set of data has two values that both appear most often. What is it called?
quiz.why_en: A set with two modes is bimodal (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: What is the median of 4, 7, 5, 4, 10?
quiz.why_en: In order they are 4, 4, 5, 7, 10 and the middle value is 5 (p.45).

quiz.stem_en: What is the median of 7, 3, 13, 1, 7, 5?
quiz.why_en: In order: 1, 3, 5, 7, 7, 13. The two middle values are 5 and 7, and halfway is 6 (p.45).

quiz.stem_en: What must you do before you can find the median?

choices.en: Put the values in order of size

quiz.why_en: The median is the middle value once the data is in order (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: Six heights add up to 834 cm. What is the mean height?
How do you work out the mean of a set of values?

choices.en: Add them all up, then divide by how many there are
Take the value that appears most
Subtract the smallest from the largest

quiz.why_en: That is the method in the worked example (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: What is the mean of 4, 7, 5, 4, 10?
A group of heights runs from 127 cm to 152 cm. What is the range?
Two groups have the same mean but one has a much larger range. What does that tell you?

choices.en: That group's values are more spread out
That group has a higher mean

quiz.why_en: The range describes how spread out a set of data is (p.42).

quiz.stem_en: Seven buckets collected $34, $0, $263, $37, $0, $42 and $51. Why is the mean a poor description of a typical bucket?

choices.en: One very large amount, $263, pulls the mean up

quiz.why_en: A single very large value pulls the mean away from what is typical (p.45).

quiz.stem_en: What does an average tell you about a set of data?

choices.en: The largest value in the set
What a typical value in the set is like
The difference between the biggest and smallest

quiz.why_en: The average represents what is typical (p.39).

quiz.stem_en: The temperature is −30 °C and rises by 5 °C. What is the new temperature?
The temperature is −30 °C and falls by 5 °C. What is the new temperature?
Which of these is an integer?
quiz.why_en: An integer is a whole number, and it can be negative (p.49).

quiz.stem_en: On a number line, what happens when you subtract?
quiz.why_en: Subtracting moves you down the number line (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: What is the difference between −6 and 4?
quiz.why_en: From −6 up to 0 is 6, then 4 more, so 10 (p.51).

quiz.stem_en: What is the difference between −6 and −2?
quiz.why_en: They are 4 apart on the number line (p.51).

quiz.stem_en: Estimate 4,825 + 3,190 by rounding each number to the nearest thousand.
quiz.why_en: 5,000 + 3,000 = 8,000, close to the exact answer 8,015 (p.49).

quiz.stem_en: Why is it useful to estimate before calculating?

choices.en: It gives the exact answer faster
It removes the need to calculate
It shows whether the exact answer is sensible

quiz.why_en: Comparing the estimate with the exact answer helps you spot mistakes (p.49).

quiz.stem_en: The dice score d is 5. What is d + 4?
quiz.why_en: Replace d with 5: 5 + 4 = 9 (p.55).

quiz.stem_en: The dice score d is 5. What is 6 − d?
Is x − 3 the same as 3 − x?

choices.en: Yes, just like x + 3 and 3 + x
No, because subtraction cannot be swapped round

quiz.why_en: Addition can be written either way round, but subtraction cannot (p.56).

quiz.stem_en: Which pair of expressions is equal?
quiz.why_en: Only the additions can be swapped round (p.56).

quiz.stem_en: A rectangle has sides s and t and a perimeter of 20 cm. What must s + t be?
quiz.why_en: s + t is half the distance round the rectangle (p.55).

quiz.stem_en: A rectangle has perimeter 20 cm and whole-centimetre sides. If s = 3 cm, what is t?
What is a variable?

choices.en: A letter standing for a value that can change
The largest number in a set

quiz.why_en: An unknown is not necessarily one fixed number but a variable (p.54).

quiz.stem_en: 3.95 is rounded to the nearest tenth. Why is the answer written as 4.0 and not as 4?

choices.en: An answer rounded to the nearest tenth always keeps one digit after the decimal point
Because 4.0 is a larger number than 4 is
Because 3.95 had to be rounded up two times over
Because the zero shows that the answer is exact

quiz.why_en: There must always be one decimal place in the answer, even when it is zero (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: 3.04 is rounded twice: once to the nearest whole number and once to the nearest tenth. What are the two answers?
quiz.why_en: Both round down, but the nearest-tenth answer keeps one decimal place (p.17).

quiz.stem_en: How many sides does a quadrilateral have?
quiz.why_en: A shape is a quadrilateral when it has four sides (p.64).

quiz.stem_en: What does it mean to say that the diagonals of a shape bisect each other?

choices.en: They meet the sides of the shape at 90 degrees
They are always the same length as each other
They never cross anywhere inside the shape
They cut each other exactly in half

quiz.why_en: To bisect means to cut exactly in half (p.64).

quiz.stem_en: A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides and all its angles are 90 degrees. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
quiz.why_en: A rectangle has one horizontal and one vertical line of symmetry (p.64).

quiz.stem_en: Side a is parallel to side e. Side g is also parallel to side e. What is true about sides a and g?

choices.en: Side a is longer than side g
Side a is parallel to side g
Side a meets side g at 90 degrees
Side a and side g must cross each other

quiz.why_en: Two lines that are both parallel to the same line are parallel to each other (p.68).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is NOT one of the seven special quadrilaterals?
quiz.why_en: The seven special quadrilaterals are the square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, isosceles trapezium, rhombus and kite (p.67).

quiz.stem_en: A square has four equal sides and all its angles are 90 degrees. How many pairs of parallel sides does it have?
quiz.why_en: A square has two pairs of parallel sides (p.65).

quiz.stem_en: How many pairs of equal angles does a rhombus have?
quiz.why_en: A rhombus has two pairs of equal angles (p.80).

quiz.stem_en: What is the perimeter of a circle called?
quiz.why_en: The perimeter of a circle is called the circumference (p.70).

quiz.stem_en: Which line joins two points on the circumference and passes through the centre of a circle?
quiz.why_en: The diameter joins two points on the circumference and goes through the centre (p.70).

quiz.stem_en: Arun draws a circle of radius 3 cm. Sofia draws a circle of diameter 60 mm. What can you say about the two circles?

choices.en: Arun's circle is the bigger one
Sofia's circle is the bigger one
You cannot compare them without measuring
They are exactly the same size

quiz.why_en: 60 mm is 6 cm, which is twice the 3 cm radius, so both circles have a diameter of 6 cm (p.73).

quiz.stem_en: You want to draw a circle of radius 4 cm with a pair of compasses. What should you do first?

choices.en: Open the compasses to 4 cm and mark the centre with a dot
Open the compasses to 8 cm and mark the centre with a dot
Draw the circumference first and then find the centre
Draw a line 4 cm long and then curve it round

quiz.why_en: You open the compasses to the radius, then put the point on the centre dot (p.71).

quiz.stem_en: Circle A has a radius of 6 cm and circle B has a radius of 2.5 cm. The two circles touch. How far apart are their centres?
quiz.why_en: The distance between the centres of two touching circles is the sum of the radii: 6 + 2.5 = 8.5 cm (p.75).

quiz.stem_en: What does the order of rotational symmetry of a shape tell you?

choices.en: The number of lines of symmetry the shape has
The number of degrees in one full turn
The number of times the shape looks the same in one full turn
The number of equal sides the shape has

quiz.why_en: The order is the number of times the shape looks the same in one full turn (p.76).

quiz.stem_en: A shape only looks the same again after a full turn. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
quiz.why_en: An isosceles trapezium only looks the same after a full turn, so its order is 1 (p.77).

quiz.stem_en: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
quiz.why_en: It fits back onto itself three times in one full turn, so the order is 3 (p.77).

quiz.stem_en: A square has four lines of symmetry. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
quiz.why_en: A square looks the same in four positions in one full turn (p.78).

quiz.stem_en: What is the bottom number of a fraction called?
quiz.why_en: The denominator is the bottom number and tells you how many equal parts the whole is split into (p.85).

quiz.stem_en: Which one of these is an improper fraction?
quiz.why_en: In 7/4 the numerator is bigger than the denominator, so the fraction is greater than one whole (p.85).

quiz.stem_en: Which mixed number is equal to the improper fraction 7/4?
quiz.why_en: 7/4 is one whole (4/4) with 3/4 left over, which is written 1 3/4 (p.85).

quiz.stem_en: Five friends share 3 cakes equally between them. What fraction of a cake does each friend get?
quiz.why_en: 3 cakes shared between 5 people is 3 divided by 5, which is 3/5 of a cake each (p.86).

quiz.stem_en: What is 3/4 of 20?
quiz.why_en: Divide by the denominator: 20 divided by 4 is 5, then multiply by the numerator: 5 x 3 = 15 (p.85).

quiz.stem_en: What is 4/3 of 12?
quiz.why_en: 12 divided by 3 is 4, then 4 x 4 = 16, which is bigger than 12 because 4/3 is an improper fraction (p.85).

quiz.stem_en: Leroy has 90 bricks and uses 3/5 of them to build a wall. How many bricks does he have left?
quiz.why_en: 3/5 of 90 is 90 divided by 5 times 3 = 54 bricks used, so 90 - 54 = 36 are left (p.87).

quiz.stem_en: What does 'per cent' mean?
quiz.why_en: Per cent means the number of parts out of every hundred (p.88).

quiz.stem_en: A man has a mass of 80 kg and 60% of that mass is water. What is the mass of the water?
quiz.why_en: 10% of 80 kg is 8 kg, so 60% is 8 x 6 = 48 kg (p.89).

quiz.stem_en: What is 45% of 240?
Song has a strip of paper 20 cm long and cuts a 5 cm piece off it. What percentage of the strip does he cut off?
quiz.why_en: 5 out of 20 is the same as 25 out of 100, so he cuts off 25% (p.90).

quiz.stem_en: What is 12/20 written in its simplest form?
quiz.why_en: Divide the numerator and the denominator by 4: 12 divided by 4 is 3 and 20 divided by 4 is 5 (p.93).

quiz.stem_en: What is 18/24 written in its simplest form?
quiz.why_en: Divide both numbers by 6: 18 divided by 6 is 3 and 24 divided by 6 is 4 (p.93).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these fractions is equal to the decimal 0.6?
quiz.why_en: The digit 6 in 0.6 stands for 6 tenths, so 0.6 is the same as 6/10 (p.94).

quiz.stem_en: What is the fraction 3/100 written as a percentage?
quiz.why_en: Per cent means parts out of every hundred, so 3/100 is 3% (p.94).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these numbers is the largest: 7/10, 50%, 0.65 or 3/5?
quiz.why_en: Written as decimals these are 0.7, 0.5, 0.65 and 0.6, so 7/10 is the largest (p.95).

quiz.stem_en: How do you find the area of a rectangle?

choices.en: Add the length to the width, then double it
Multiply the length by the number of sides
Multiply the length by the width
Add all four side lengths together

quiz.why_en: The area of a rectangle is the width multiplied by the length (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: A rectangle is 8 m long and 4 m wide. What is its area?
quiz.why_en: 8 × 4 = 32, and the lengths are in metres so the area is 32 m² (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: A rectangle 8 m by 4 m is cut in half along a diagonal. What is the area of each triangle?
quiz.why_en: The rectangle covers 8 × 4 = 32 m² and each triangle is half of it, so 32 ÷ 2 = 16 m² (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: A rectangle is cut in half along a diagonal. How does the area of one triangle compare with the area of the rectangle?

choices.en: It is one quarter of it

quiz.why_en: Cutting a rectangle in half makes two equal triangles, so each one is half of the rectangle (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: A triangle with an area of 9 cm² is half of a rectangle. What is the area of that rectangle?
quiz.why_en: The triangle is half the rectangle, so you double it: 9 × 2 = 18 cm² (p.105).

quiz.stem_en: Jo cuts a 5 cm square of dough in half to make a triangular biscuit. What is the area of one biscuit?
quiz.why_en: The square covers 5 × 5 = 25 cm² and the biscuit is half of it, so 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5 cm² (p.105).

quiz.stem_en: A triangular lawn is half of a rectangle 5 m by 7 m. Which is the smallest bag of seed that covers it: A (10 m²), B (17 m²), C (20 m²) or D (35 m²)?
quiz.why_en: The rectangle is 5 × 7 = 35 m², so the lawn is 17.5 m², which is too big for bag B but fits inside bag C (p.111).

quiz.stem_en: You are estimating the area of a triangle drawn on a centimetre square grid. What do you do with a square that the triangle only half covers?

choices.en: Count it as one whole square
Count it as half a square

quiz.why_en: A square that is half covered counts as half a square, so the part squares can be put together to make whole ones (p.103).

quiz.stem_en: A triangle is drawn inside a rectangle 8 cm by 4 cm so that it is exactly as wide and as tall as the rectangle. About what is the area of the triangle?
quiz.why_en: The rectangle covers 8 × 4 = 32 cm² and counting squares shows the triangle covers about half of it, so about 16 cm² (p.103).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a unit of area?
quiz.why_en: Units of area are square units such as mm², cm², m² and km² (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: How many minutes are there in 0.1 of an hour?
quiz.why_en: There are 60 minutes in an hour, and one tenth of 60 is 6 (p.107).

quiz.stem_en: Convert 3.7 hours into hours and minutes.
quiz.why_en: Keep the 3 whole hours, then 0.7 × 60 = 42 minutes (p.107).

quiz.stem_en: Write 9.25 hours as hours and minutes.
quiz.why_en: 0.25 × 60 = 15, so 9.25 hours is 9 hours and 15 minutes (p.111).

quiz.stem_en: Four children share 5 hours on a games console equally between them. How long does each child get?
quiz.why_en: 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25 hours, and 0.25 × 60 = 15, so each child gets 1 hour and 15 minutes (p.108).

quiz.stem_en: Five groups share a basketball court equally for 12 hours. How long does each group get in hours and minutes?
quiz.why_en: 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 hours, and 0.4 × 60 = 24, so each group gets 2 hours and 24 minutes (p.111).

quiz.stem_en: Why is 12.5 hours NOT the same as 12 hours and 5 minutes?

choices.en: Because 12.5 hours really means 12 hours and 50 minutes
Because 0.5 of an hour is 30 minutes, not 5 minutes
Because hours are always written as whole numbers
Because 0.5 of an hour has been rounded up to 5 minutes

quiz.why_en: The figures after the point are parts of an hour, and 0.5 × 60 = 30 minutes (p.109).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is equivalent to 6.075?
quiz.why_en: In 6.075 the 7 is worth 0.07 and the 5 is worth 0.005 (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: In 37.844 = 30 + 7 + ? + 0.04 + 0.004, what is the missing number?
quiz.why_en: The 8 is the first digit after the point, so it is worth 0.8 (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: Which two of these numbers have a total of exactly 1: 0.80, 0.08, 0.88, 0.02, 0.12, 0.22?
quiz.why_en: 0.88 + 0.12 = 1.00, while the other pairs give 1.02, 0.10 and 0.92 (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: Find the sum of all the numbers less than 5.5 in this list: 5.05, 5.55, 5.115, 5.5, 5.555.
When you add or subtract decimals in columns, what must line up?

choices.en: The last digits on the right
The first digits on the left
The largest digits in each number

quiz.why_en: Lining up the decimal points keeps digits of the same value in the same column (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: Why is 10 written as 10.00 before subtracting 7.58?

choices.en: Because every subtraction has to end in two zeros
Because 7.58 must be changed to 7.60 first
So that both numbers have the same number of decimal places

quiz.why_en: Trailing zeros give both numbers the same number of decimal places so the columns match (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 10.00 − 7.58.
quiz.why_en: 10.00 − 7.58 = 2.42, which is close to the estimate of 10 − 7.6 = 2.4 (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 14.8 + 5.678.
Calculate 56.1 − 26.64.
Ahmed writes 0.7 + 0.41 = 0.48. What is the correct answer?
quiz.why_en: 0.7 is the same as 0.70, so 0.70 + 0.41 = 1.11; Ahmed lined up the last digits instead of the points (p.116).

quiz.stem_en: Darius packs two suitcases weighing 11.284 kg and 8.65 kg. He is allowed 20 kg. How far under the 20 kg limit is he?
Which of these numbers is a common denominator for 9/5 and 3/4?
quiz.why_en: 20 is in the list of multiples of 5 and also in the list of multiples of 4 (p.118).

quiz.stem_en: What must you do first before you can add 9/5 and 3/4?

choices.en: Add the numerators and the denominators
Change both fractions into mixed numbers
Rewrite both fractions with the same denominator

quiz.why_en: Fractions can only be added when their parts are the same size, so you find a common denominator first (p.118).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 9/5 + 3/4.
Leroy colours 1/4 of a circle and 1/6 of the same circle. What fraction of the circle is left white?
Chipo says 2/3 + 3/5 = 19/15. Leke says 2/3 + 3/5 = 1 4/15. Who is right?

choices.en: Only Chipo, because 1 4/15 is too small
Both of them, because 19/15 and 1 4/15 are equal
Only Leke, because 19/15 is not a fraction
Neither of them, the answer is 5/8

quiz.why_en: 10/15 + 9/15 = 19/15, and 15/15 makes one whole with 4/15 left, so 19/15 is the same as 1 4/15 (p.119).

quiz.stem_en: What does probability tell you?

choices.en: How long something takes to happen
How many times you have played a game
How likely something is to happen
How far away something is from you

quiz.why_en: Probability is a number that tells us how likely an event is to happen (p.123).

quiz.stem_en: Ten cards show 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 1, 4, 6, 7 and 8. One card is taken without looking. What is the probability of taking a 2?
quiz.why_en: There is only one 2 among the ten cards, so the probability is 1 out of 10 (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: Ten cards show 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 1, 4, 6, 7 and 8. What is the probability of taking a card with a value higher than 4?
quiz.why_en: The cards higher than 4 are 7, 9, 6, 7 and 8, so 5 out of 10, which is 50% (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: Ten cards show 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 1, 4, 6, 7 and 8. What is the probability of taking a card that is NOT a 3?
quiz.why_en: None of the ten cards is a 3, so all 10 out of 10 cards work, which is 100% (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: A weather forecast gives the chance of rain each hour: 13% at 0600, 20% at 1300, 32% at 1800 and 21% at 2200. When is rain most likely?
quiz.why_en: 32% is the highest of the four percentages, so rain is most likely at 1800 (p.124).

quiz.stem_en: What does it mean if two events are mutually exclusive?

choices.en: They have exactly the same probability
They are both impossible to happen
They cannot happen at the same time

quiz.why_en: Mutually exclusive events are events that cannot happen at the same time (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: A spinner has the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 on it. Which pair of events is mutually exclusive?

choices.en: Spin a 5, and spin a number less than 4
Spin a 5, and spin a number greater than 2
Spin a number greater than 2, and spin a number less than 4
Spin a 3, and spin a number less than 4

quiz.why_en: No number is both a 5 and less than 4, while a 5 is greater than 2 and a 3 is less than 4 (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: Tickets numbered 1 to 30 are in a bag. A big prize needs a ticket that is both odd and a multiple of 10. What is the chance of winning the big prize?

choices.en: There is no chance at all

quiz.why_en: The multiples of 10 are 10, 20 and 30, and none of them is odd, so no ticket wins the big prize (p.127).

quiz.stem_en: You roll a red dice and a blue dice. Which pair of events CANNOT happen at the same time?

choices.en: Rolling a double, and getting a 6 on the red dice
Rolling a double, and the two scores adding up to an even number
Rolling a double, and the blue score being greater than the red
Getting a 6 on the red dice, and the two scores adding to an even number

quiz.why_en: A double means the two scores are equal, so the blue score cannot be greater than the red one (p.129).

quiz.stem_en: A spinner shows the numbers 1 to 8. Event 1: it lands on 5. Event 2: it lands on a number less than 6. Event 3: it lands on a multiple of 3. Which two events are mutually exclusive?
quiz.why_en: The multiples of 3 are 3 and 6, and neither of them is 5, so events 1 and 3 cannot both happen (p.131).

quiz.stem_en: A spinner is most likely to land on red 4 times, blue 3 times and yellow 1 time in every 8 spins. What is most likely after 16 spins?
quiz.why_en: 16 spins is double 8 spins, so double each prediction: 8 red, 6 blue and 2 yellow (p.129).

quiz.stem_en: A spinner is most likely to land on red 4 times in every 8 spins. How many times is it most likely to land on red in 200 spins?
quiz.why_en: 4 out of 8 spins is half of them, and half of 200 is 100 (p.129).

quiz.stem_en: A bag holds 10 objects and 3 of them are blue. One object is taken and put back 20 times. How many blue objects would you expect to take?
quiz.why_en: Blue is 3 out of every 10 objects, and 3 out of 10 of the 20 turns is 6 (p.129).

quiz.stem_en: In a probability experiment, what is an outcome?

choices.en: The number of trials you carry out
A list of the events that are impossible
The prediction you made before you started

quiz.why_en: An outcome is the result of one trial in a probability experiment (p.123).

quiz.stem_en: Keran flips a coin and records 24 heads up and 16 tails up. How many trials did she carry out?
quiz.why_en: Every flip is one trial, so 24 + 16 = 40 trials (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: Keran flips a coin and records 24 heads up and 16 tails up. What is the experimental probability of the coin landing tails up?
quiz.why_en: Tails up happened 16 times in 40 trials, so the experimental probability is 16 out of 40, or 40% (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: What does the word 'product' mean in mathematics?

choices.en: The answer when numbers are added together
The amount left over after a division
The answer when numbers are multiplied together
The number you are dividing by

quiz.why_en: The product is the result of a multiplication (p.135).

quiz.stem_en: In the calculation 552 ÷ 24, which number is the divisor?

choices.en: 552, because it is the largest number
480, because it is used in the working
24, because it is the number you divide by

quiz.why_en: The divisor is the number you are dividing by (p.139).

quiz.stem_en: What is 1347 × 8?
What is 552 ÷ 24?
Lexi estimates that 1499 × 59 is about 900 000. Why is her estimate wrong?

choices.en: 1500 × 60 = 9000, so her estimate is far too big
She should have rounded 1499 down to 1000 instead
1500 × 60 = 90 000, so her estimate is ten times too big
The real answer is larger than 900 000, not smaller

quiz.why_en: Rounding to 1500 × 60 gives 90 000, so 900 000 is ten times too large (p.136).

quiz.stem_en: What is 5489 × 30?
A heart beats about 79 times each minute. About how many times does it beat in one day?
What is 960 ÷ 15?
quiz.why_en: Divide by the factors of 15: 960 ÷ 3 = 320 and 320 ÷ 5 = 64 (p.140).

quiz.stem_en: What is the remainder when 493 is divided by 7?
The answer to 493 ÷ 7 is 70 remainder 3. How is the same answer written as a mixed number?
quiz.why_en: The remainder becomes the numerator and the divisor becomes the denominator (p.139).

quiz.stem_en: How can you tell that a whole number is divisible by 3?

choices.en: The sum of its digits is a multiple of 3
It ends in the digit 3, 6 or 9
Its last two digits make a multiple of 3

quiz.why_en: The test of divisibility for 3 uses the sum of the digits (p.142).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these numbers is divisible by 3?
quiz.why_en: 4 + 3 + 7 + 1 + 9 = 24, which is a multiple of 3 (p.143).

quiz.stem_en: Which test tells you that a whole number is divisible by 6?

choices.en: The number is even and it ends in the digit 6
The digits of the number add up to exactly 6
The number is even and its digits add up to a multiple of 3
The number is odd and it is also divisible by 3

quiz.why_en: 6 = 2 × 3, so the number must pass the test for 2 and the test for 3 (p.144).

quiz.stem_en: Oscar's number is between 200 and 220. It is divisible by 6 and its digits add up to 3. What is his number?
A chef has 15 boxes of apples with 16 apples in each box. She uses 3 apples for each pie. How many pies can she make?
Jamila checks the calculation 117 ÷ 9 = 14 using the inverse operation. What does she find?

choices.en: 9 × 14 = 117, so the answer given is correct
9 × 14 = 126, not 117, so the answer should be 13
117 × 9 = 14, so the answer given is correct

quiz.why_en: The inverse of dividing by 9 is multiplying by 9, and 9 × 13 = 117 (p.145).

quiz.stem_en: What does the capacity of a container tell you?

choices.en: The amount of liquid that is in it now
The total area of all of its faces
The most it can hold when it is full
The height of the container in centimetres

quiz.why_en: Capacity is the maximum amount a container can hold (p.154).

quiz.stem_en: A jug is marked up to 600 ml and the water reaches the 500 ml mark. What is the volume of the water?
quiz.why_en: The volume is read from the mark the water reaches (p.154).

quiz.stem_en: A jug with a capacity of 600 ml holds 500 ml of water. What volume of water must be added to fill it to capacity?
quiz.why_en: 600 − 500 = 100 ml is still empty (p.154).

quiz.stem_en: What is the surface area of a 3D shape?

choices.en: The amount of space inside the shape
The total area of all its faces
The number of faces the shape has
The lengths of all its edges added up

quiz.why_en: Surface area is the total area of every face of the shape (p.151).

quiz.stem_en: Deema sketches the net of a cuboid. It is made of 4 rectangles and 2 squares. How many faces does the cuboid have?
quiz.why_en: A cuboid has six faces, so its net has six pieces (p.150).

quiz.stem_en: A triangular prism has five faces and two of them are triangles. What shape are the other three faces?
quiz.why_en: In a prism the two identical ends are joined by rectangles (p.151).

quiz.stem_en: A square based pyramid has five faces and one of them is a square. What shape are the other four faces?
quiz.why_en: Four triangles rise from the square base to meet at a point (p.161).

quiz.stem_en: What is a compound 3D shape?

choices.en: A 3D shape that has no flat faces at all
A shape made from two or more simpler shapes
A flat pattern that folds up into a 3D shape
A 3D shape with two identical parallel faces

quiz.why_en: A compound shape is built from simpler shapes joined together (p.149).

quiz.stem_en: What is a net of a 3D shape?

choices.en: A drawing of the shape on isometric paper
The total area of all the faces of the shape
A flat pattern of faces that folds into the shape
The amount of space inside the shape

quiz.why_en: A net shows every face laid out flat, ready to be folded up (p.150).

quiz.stem_en: How many millilitres are there in 1 litre?
Which of these is the same volume as 3200 ml?
quiz.why_en: 3200 ml is 3 litres and 200 ml, which is written 3.2 litres (p.155).

quiz.stem_en: Chipo needs 2.3 litres of milk but her only measuring jug has a capacity of 500 ml. How can she measure it out?

choices.en: Fill the jug 23 times right to the top
Fill the jug 4 times, then add another 300 ml
Fill the jug twice, then add another 300 ml
Fill the jug 3 times, then add another 200 ml

quiz.why_en: 2.3 litres is 2300 ml, and 4 × 500 = 2000 ml, leaving 300 ml (p.157).

quiz.stem_en: A fish tank has a capacity of 120 litres. Water is poured in until the tank is three quarters full. What is the volume of the water?
A hexagonal prism has 2 identical hexagonal end faces joined by rectangles. How many rectangular faces does it have?
quiz.why_en: A hexagon has six sides, and each side needs one rectangle to join the two ends (p.152).

quiz.stem_en: What does a ratio compare?

choices.en: A part with the whole amount
The total of a set of values

quiz.why_en: Ratio compares part to part, such as apples to oranges (p.166).

quiz.stem_en: What does a proportion compare?

choices.en: A part with the whole amount

quiz.why_en: Proportion compares a part with the whole, as in '1 in every 4' (p.169).

quiz.stem_en: What is the ratio 21 : 14 written in its simplest form?
quiz.why_en: Divide both parts by 7: 21 ÷ 7 = 3 and 14 ÷ 7 = 2 (p.167).

quiz.stem_en: What is the ratio 150 : 25 written in its simplest form?
quiz.why_en: Divide both parts by 25: 150 ÷ 25 = 6 and 25 ÷ 25 = 1 (p.167).

quiz.stem_en: Which number is missing? 2 : 3 = 12 : ?
quiz.why_en: 2 was multiplied by 6, so 3 × 6 = 18 (p.167).

quiz.stem_en: Which number is missing? 5 : 7 = ? : 21
quiz.why_en: 7 was multiplied by 3, so 5 × 3 = 15 (p.167).

quiz.stem_en: In a survey the ratio of people who preferred apples to bananas was 3 : 5, and 45 people preferred bananas. How many people took part altogether?
Pierre plants 4 carrots for every 3 onions. He plants 48 carrots. How many onions does he plant?
quiz.why_en: 48 ÷ 4 = 12, so the ratio is multiplied by 12 and 3 × 12 = 36 onions (p.168).

quiz.stem_en: The ratio of girls to boys in a competition is 3 : 2 and 42 girls take part. How many children take part altogether?
quiz.why_en: 42 ÷ 3 = 14, so there are 2 × 14 = 28 boys, and 42 + 28 = 70 children (p.168).

quiz.stem_en: Three melons cost $2. What is the cost of 15 melons?
350 grams of pasta is enough for 4 people. How much pasta is needed for 12 people?
quiz.why_en: 4 × 3 = 12, so multiply the pasta by 3: 350 × 3 = 1050 grams (p.170).

quiz.stem_en: An ice cream recipe for 8 people uses 500 ml of milk. How much milk is needed for 4 people?
quiz.why_en: 4 is half of 8, so halve the milk: 500 ÷ 2 = 250 ml (p.171).

quiz.stem_en: Two quantities are in direct proportion. What happens to the second one when the first one doubles?
quiz.why_en: In direct proportion both quantities change in the same ratio (p.169).

quiz.stem_en: A model car is built to a scale of 1 : 24 and the model is 170 mm long. How long is the real car?
quiz.why_en: The real car is 24 times as long: 170 × 24 = 4080 mm (p.172).

quiz.stem_en: When is a ratio in its simplest form?

choices.en: When both of its parts are even numbers
When the two parts add up to ten
When no number above 1 divides both parts
When the first part is larger than the second

quiz.why_en: The parts cannot be reduced any further by dividing by the same number (p.167).

quiz.stem_en: Rectangle A is 5 cm long and 2 cm wide. Rectangle B is an enlargement of A with lengths in the ratio A : B = 1 : 2. What is the perimeter of B?
quiz.why_en: B is 10 cm by 4 cm, so its perimeter is 10 + 4 + 10 + 4 = 28 cm (p.172).

quiz.stem_en: What is a protractor used for?

choices.en: Measuring the length of straight lines
Drawing circles of an exact size
Checking that two lines are parallel

quiz.why_en: A ruler is used for straight lines, but a protractor is the instrument for measuring and drawing angles (p.178).

quiz.stem_en: A protractor has an outside ring and an inside ring of numbers. Which ring do you read when the angle opens clockwise from 0°?

choices.en: Either ring, as they always give the same number
The ring that starts at 90° instead of 0°

quiz.why_en: When you measure clockwise from 0° you use the numbers on the outside circle (p.178).

quiz.stem_en: A circular protractor is marked with degrees all the way around its edge. What range of degrees does it show?
quiz.why_en: A circular protractor has 0° to 360° marked around its edge, which is one full turn (p.178).

quiz.stem_en: Where must the centre of the protractor be placed when you measure an angle?

choices.en: At the far end of the longer arm
Just outside the angle, next to the arms
On the point where the two arms meet

quiz.why_en: The centre of the protractor goes on the point of the angle, where the two arms meet (p.179).

quiz.stem_en: When you measure an angle, one arm must line up exactly with which mark on the protractor?
quiz.why_en: One arm has to sit exactly on 0°, otherwise every number you read will be wrong (p.179).

quiz.stem_en: You want to draw an angle of 120°. What should you do first?

choices.en: Mark a point 120 mm along from the corner
Draw a horizontal line with a ruler
Draw an arc and write 120° on it
Count 120 small marks on the protractor

quiz.why_en: You start by drawing a horizontal line, then put the centre of the protractor on one end of it (p.179).

quiz.stem_en: You have used a protractor to mark 120° on your paper. What do you do next?

choices.en: Measure the mark again with the inside numbers
Rub out the horizontal line you started with
Join the mark to the end of the line, then label the angle
Slide the protractor along and mark another 120°

quiz.why_en: Take the protractor away, join your mark to the end of the line, then draw an arc and write 120° (p.179).

quiz.stem_en: A wheelchair ramp is only allowed if the angle of the ramp is no more than 20°. A ramp measures 24°. What can you say about it?

choices.en: It is allowed, because 24° is smaller than 90°
It is allowed, because 24° is quite close to 20°
It is not allowed, because the angle is not 90°
It is not allowed, because 24° is more than 20°

quiz.why_en: The rule is no more than 20°, and 24° is bigger than 20°, so this ramp is not allowed (p.182).

quiz.stem_en: What do the three angles inside any triangle add up to?
quiz.why_en: Tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and putting them together makes a straight line of 180° (p.184).

quiz.stem_en: Two angles of a triangle are 30° and 70°. What is the size of the third angle?
quiz.why_en: 30 + 70 = 100, and 180 − 100 = 80, so the third angle is 80° (p.184).

quiz.stem_en: A triangle has angles of 80° and 40°. What is the size of the third angle?
quiz.why_en: 80 + 40 = 120, and 180 − 120 = 60, so the third angle is 60° (p.184).

quiz.stem_en: All three angles in an equilateral triangle are equal. How big is each one?
quiz.why_en: Three equal angles share 180°, and 180 ÷ 3 = 60, so each angle is 60° (p.186).

quiz.stem_en: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles of 50°. What is the size of the third angle?
quiz.why_en: The two equal angles give 50 + 50 = 100, and 180 − 100 = 80, so the third angle is 80° (p.185).

quiz.stem_en: A right-angled triangle has a right angle of 90° and another angle of 28°. What is the third angle?
quiz.why_en: 90 + 28 = 118, and 180 − 118 = 62, so the third angle is 62° (p.185).

quiz.stem_en: Angles x, y and z sit side by side on a straight line. Angle x is 55° and angle y is 60°. What is angle z?
quiz.why_en: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: 55 + 60 = 115, and 180 − 115 = 65 (p.182).

quiz.stem_en: An angle of 127° and angle a sit side by side on a straight line. What is the size of angle a?
quiz.why_en: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so a = 180 − 127 = 53° (p.187).

quiz.stem_en: How do you multiply a proper fraction by a whole number?

choices.en: Multiply the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator.
Multiply the denominator by the whole number and keep the numerator.
Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the whole number.
Add the whole number to the numerator and keep the denominator.

quiz.why_en: Multiplying is repeated addition, so only the numerator grows while the size of each part stays the same (p.193).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 3/5 × 2.
quiz.why_en: 3 × 2 = 6 and the denominator stays 5, so the answer is 6/5 (p.193).

quiz.stem_en: Which multiplication gives the same answer as 2/8 + 2/8 + 2/8 + 2/8 + 2/8?
quiz.why_en: There are five lots of 2/8, so the addition can be written as 2/8 × 5 = 10/8 (p.193).

quiz.stem_en: How do you divide a proper fraction by a whole number?

choices.en: Multiply the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator.
Divide the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator.
Divide the numerator and the denominator by the whole number.
Multiply the denominator by the whole number and keep the numerator.

quiz.why_en: Dividing cuts every part into smaller parts, so the whole ends up with more parts in it (p.193).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 2/3 ÷ 4. Give your answer in its simplest form.
quiz.why_en: Each third splits into 4, giving 2/12, and 2/12 simplifies to 1/6 (p.193).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 4/5 ÷ 2. Give your answer in its simplest form.
quiz.why_en: 5 × 2 = 10, so the answer is 4/10, which simplifies to 2/5 (p.194).

quiz.stem_en: Oscar, Bruno and Ali share 2/3 of a large pie equally between the three of them. What fraction of the whole pie does each boy get?
quiz.why_en: 2/3 ÷ 3 splits each third into three, giving 2/9 of the whole pie each (p.194).

quiz.stem_en: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides. Its perimeter is 26.25 metres. How long is one side?
quiz.why_en: 26.25 ÷ 5 = 5.25, and the estimate 25 ÷ 5 = 5 shows the answer is about right (p.201).

quiz.stem_en: What is 10/3 written as a mixed number?
quiz.why_en: There are three whole lots of 3/3 in 10/3 with 1/3 left over, so 10/3 = 3 1/3 (p.195).

quiz.stem_en: Write 2/12 in its simplest form.
quiz.why_en: Both numbers halve: 2 ÷ 2 = 1 and 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so 2/12 = 1/6 (p.193).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these fractions is an improper fraction?
quiz.why_en: In 10/8 the numerator is bigger than the denominator, so it is worth more than one whole (p.194).

quiz.stem_en: Why should you always work out an estimate before multiplying decimals?

choices.en: Because the estimate is the exact answer you need
Because decimals cannot be multiplied in any other way
Because rounding makes the numbers quicker to write down
Because it gives a rough answer to check the real one against

quiz.why_en: Rounding both numbers gives a rough answer, so you can see whether your real answer is sensible (p.197).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 45.1 × 5.
A meal costs $15.25 at a restaurant and 12 people each buy one meal. What is the total cost of the meals?
Calculate 37.2 ÷ 4.
quiz.why_en: 4 × 9 = 36 leaves 1.2, and 1.2 ÷ 4 = 0.3, so the answer is 9.3 (p.200).

quiz.stem_en: Ella, Kiki and Mandy spend $29.52 on food and share the cost equally between the three of them. How much does Mandy pay?
quiz.why_en: 29.52 ÷ 3 = 9.84, and the estimate 30 ÷ 3 = 10 shows the answer is about right (p.201).

quiz.stem_en: On a dot plot, what does a column of five dots above the score 7 tell you?

choices.en: The total of all the scores was 7
The highest score on the test was 5

quiz.why_en: A dot plot uses one dot for each item, so five dots is a frequency of five (p.205).

quiz.stem_en: A farmer counted the peas in 72 pods. Grouped in fives: 1-5 peas in 10 pods, 6-10 in 28 pods, 11-15 in 29 pods, 16-20 in 5 pods. Which bar is the tallest?
quiz.why_en: 29 pods is the largest frequency, so 11-15 has the tallest bar (p.207).

quiz.stem_en: A farmer counted the peas in 72 pods. Grouped in fives: 1-5 peas in 10 pods, 6-10 in 28 pods, 11-15 in 29 pods, 16-20 in 5 pods. How many pods held more than 10 peas?
quiz.why_en: Add the two groups above 10: 29 + 5 = 34 pods (p.207).

quiz.stem_en: A 100 square waffle diagram shows the choices of 20 children. How many squares stand for one child?
quiz.why_en: 100 ÷ 20 = 5, so each child fills 5 squares (p.207).

quiz.stem_en: Of 20 children, 5 chose football, 9 chose basketball, 3 chose table tennis, 1 chose volleyball and 2 chose cricket. What percentage chose basketball?
quiz.why_en: Each child is 5 squares out of 100, so 9 children is 45 squares, or 45% (p.208).

quiz.stem_en: Of 20 children, 5 chose football, 9 chose basketball, 3 chose table tennis and 2 chose cricket. The rest chose volleyball. What percentage of the waffle diagram is volleyball?
quiz.why_en: 20 - 19 = 1 child chose volleyball, and one child is 5 squares out of 100 (p.208).

quiz.stem_en: A pie chart is drawn for favourite animals: elephant 1, tiger 2, giraffe 2. Into how many equal sections is the circle divided?
quiz.why_en: The total frequency is 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, so the circle is split into 5 sections (p.208).

quiz.stem_en: Asif asked 10 friends how they travel to school: 5 walk, 1 goes by car, 3 go by bus and 1 cycles. What fraction of his pie chart is the walking section?
quiz.why_en: 5 out of 10 friends walk, and 5 tenths is one half (p.210).

quiz.stem_en: You want to find out whether any candidate in an election won more than 50% of the votes. Which chart answers that most directly?

choices.en: A pie chart, because each slice is a share of the whole
A dot plot, because it shows one dot for every vote cast
A line graph, because it shows how the votes changed over time
A scatter graph, because it compares two different measurements

quiz.why_en: A pie chart shows each part of the whole circle, so you can see if a slice is more than half (p.211).

quiz.stem_en: A class measured how high they could jump. Grouped: 16-20 cm 3 children, 21-25 cm 8, 26-30 cm 14, 31-35 cm 5, 36-40 cm 1. How many jumped 26 cm or higher?
quiz.why_en: Add the top three groups: 14 + 5 + 1 = 20 children (p.213).

quiz.stem_en: Dee's pulse rate was 66 at 0 minutes, 102 at 10, 102 at 20, 118 at 30, 106 at 40, 130 at 50, 130 at 60, 88 at 70 and 68 at 80 minutes. When was it 118?
quiz.why_en: The reading of 118 beats per minute was taken at 30 minutes (p.214).

quiz.stem_en: Dee's pulse rate was 106 beats per minute at 40 minutes and 130 beats per minute at 50 minutes. What happened between those two times?

choices.en: It stayed level at 106 beats per minute
It fell by 24 beats per minute
It fell by 12 beats per minute
It rose by 24 beats per minute

quiz.why_en: 130 - 106 = 24, so the line goes up by 24 beats per minute (p.214).

quiz.stem_en: Which investigation is best shown on a line graph?

choices.en: How quickly hot water cools down to room temperature
Which sport is the most popular one in our class
What the most common shoe size in the classroom is
Whether taller people also tend to have longer arms

quiz.why_en: A line graph is for something measured again and again over time, such as cooling water (p.219).

quiz.stem_en: Eleven plants had heights of 6, 8, 9, 11, 11, 12, 13, 15, 15, 17, 18 cm and leaf counts of 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9. What link does the scatter graph show?

choices.en: The taller the plant, the fewer leaves it has
The taller the plant, the more leaves it has
Height and number of leaves are not linked at all
Every plant has exactly the same number of leaves

quiz.why_en: The points rise from left to right: the 6 cm plant has 2 leaves and the 18 cm plant has 9 (p.218).

quiz.stem_en: What is a line of best fit on a scatter graph?

choices.en: A line joining the highest point to the lowest point
A line drawn above every one of the plotted points
A straight line through the middle, with as many points above as below
A curved line that passes through all the plotted points

quiz.why_en: The line needs the right slope and about the same number of points each side (p.217).

quiz.stem_en: Izzy plotted hand span against foot length and drew a line of best fit. A new child has a hand span of 17 cm. How should she estimate their foot length?

choices.en: Read across from 17 cm to the highest point on the graph
Count how many points sit above 17 cm on the graph
Add 17 cm to the longest foot length in her class
Go from 17 cm to the line of best fit, then read the other axis

quiz.why_en: The line of best fit lets you estimate a measurement you have not taken (p.218).

quiz.stem_en: Which operation must be done first in 3 × 4 + 6?

choices.en: Either one, the answer is the same

quiz.why_en: Multiplication comes before addition in the order of operations (p.224).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate 6 + 3 × 4.
quiz.why_en: Multiply first: 3 × 4 = 12, then 6 + 12 = 18 (p.224).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate (6 + 3) × 4.
quiz.why_en: Brackets first: 6 + 3 = 9, then 9 × 4 = 36 (p.224).

quiz.stem_en: What do brackets tell you to do in a calculation?

choices.en: Leave out the numbers that are inside them
Work through the whole calculation from left to right
Save the multiplication until the very last step
Work out the part inside them before anything else

quiz.why_en: Brackets come first in the order of operations (p.224).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate (3 + 7) ÷ 10.
quiz.why_en: Brackets first: 3 + 7 = 10, then 10 ÷ 10 = 1 (p.225).

quiz.stem_en: Using the numbers 6, 2 and 5 in that order, which calculation gives 40?
quiz.why_en: 8 × 5 = 40, while the others give 16, 42 and 17 (p.225).

quiz.stem_en: Which one of these statements is TRUE?
quiz.why_en: Both sides come to 25, while the other three pairs give 6 and 10, 14 and 10, 27 and 17 (p.226).

quiz.stem_en: The associative rule lets you group numbers in any order. Which pair of operations does it work for?
quiz.why_en: Only numbers that are all added or all multiplied can be regrouped freely (p.226).

quiz.stem_en: Use the distributive rule to work out 5 × (70 + 1).
quiz.why_en: 5 × 70 = 350 and 5 × 1 = 5, so the total is 355 (p.226).

quiz.stem_en: Use the distributive rule to work out 8 × 93.
Which line shows the distributive rule used correctly for 6 × (60 - 3)?
quiz.why_en: Both parts must be multiplied by 6: 360 - 18 = 342, which is 6 × 57 (p.226).

quiz.stem_en: Calculate (14 - 6) × (3 + 1).
quiz.why_en: Both brackets first: 8 × 4 = 32 (p.227).

quiz.stem_en: When you write down a pair of coordinates, which number comes first?

choices.en: The larger of the two numbers
The positive number, if there is one

quiz.why_en: Coordinates are always written with the x-axis number first (p.231).

quiz.stem_en: Where is the point (-3, 2) on a coordinate grid?

choices.en: 3 squares right of zero and 2 squares down
3 squares left of zero and 2 squares up
3 squares left of zero and 2 squares down
2 squares right of zero and 3 squares up

quiz.why_en: A negative x means left and a positive y means up (p.232).

quiz.stem_en: J is at (-2, 2), K is at (-2, -1) and L is at (1, -1). Where must M be so that J, K, L and M are the vertices of a square?
quiz.why_en: JK and KL are both 3 squares long, so M sits above L at (1, 2) (p.234).

quiz.stem_en: What does it mean to translate a shape?

choices.en: To turn it around a fixed point on the grid
To flip it over onto the other side of a line
To make it bigger or smaller than it was
To slide it left or right and up or down

quiz.why_en: A translation slides the shape without turning it (p.231).

quiz.stem_en: Point P is at (-2, 1). The shape is translated 2 squares right and 1 square up. Where is P' now?
Point S is at (3, 1). The shape is translated 2 squares left and 5 squares down. Where is S' now?
Lukman repeats the same translation on a kite. One marked vertex is at (1, 7) on the 1st kite and (3, 6) on the 2nd. Where is it on the 3rd?
quiz.why_en: Each step adds 2 to x and subtracts 1 from y, so (3, 6) becomes (5, 5) (p.236).

quiz.stem_en: A kite is translated the same way each time. A marked vertex is at (1, 7) on the 1st kite and (3, 6) on the 2nd. Where is it on the 5th kite?
quiz.why_en: Four steps of 2 right and 1 down give 1 + 8 = 9 and 7 - 4 = 3 (p.236).

quiz.stem_en: How do you reflect a shape in a mirror line?

choices.en: Put each vertex the same distance the other side of the line, then join them
Turn the whole shape a quarter turn about a point on the mirror line
Slide the whole shape sideways until it touches the mirror line
Draw the shape again the same distance further along the mirror line

quiz.why_en: Every vertex must end up the same distance from the mirror line on the other side (p.238).

quiz.stem_en: What is a diagonal mirror line?

choices.en: A mirror line that runs straight across the page
A mirror line at 45 degrees to a horizontal or vertical line
A mirror line that passes through the centre of the shape
A mirror line that is longer than the shape being reflected

quiz.why_en: A diagonal mirror line sits at 45 degrees to the horizontal and the vertical (p.237).

quiz.stem_en: A shape and its image sit side by side, each the same distance from a vertical line and facing opposite ways. Which transformation is this?

choices.en: A reflection in a vertical mirror line

quiz.why_en: Equal distances either side of the line and a flipped shape describe a reflection (p.240).

quiz.stem_en: What is the centre of rotation?

choices.en: The middle point of the shape that is being turned
The point where the x-axis and the y-axis cross
The corner of the shape that travels the furthest
The fixed point that the shape is turned about

quiz.why_en: The centre of rotation is the point the shape turns around (p.241).

quiz.stem_en: A rotation of 90 degrees is the same as which part of a full turn?
quiz.why_en: 90 degrees is a quarter turn (p.242).

quiz.stem_en: Which sentence describes a rotation that goes anticlockwise?

choices.en: It turns the shape the same way as the hands of a clock
It turns the shape the opposite way to the hands of a clock
It flips the shape over onto its other side
It slides the shape across without turning it at all

quiz.why_en: Anticlockwise means turning against the direction a clock's hands travel (p.243).

quiz.stem_en: What are corresponding vertices?

choices.en: Two vertices that are next to each other on the same shape
The vertices that lie exactly on the mirror line or the centre
Vertices in the same position on the shape before and after a move
The two vertices that end up furthest apart once a shape is moved

quiz.why_en: A vertex and its image match, so A corresponds with A' (p.244).

quiz.stem_en: You join each vertex of a triangle to its corresponding vertex after a move, and all the joining lines are parallel. Which move could it NOT have been?

choices.en: A translation of 3 squares right and 2 squares down
A reflection in a vertical mirror line
A reflection in a horizontal mirror line
A rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about a centre C

quiz.why_en: After a rotation the lines joining corresponding vertices are never parallel (p.245).
